children.description: composite: true + incremental: true writes a .tsbuildinfo file — subsequent builds only recheck files that changed, dramatically cutting CI type-check time.

children.title: Zod schemas
children.description: Zod validates data at runtime and infers TypeScript types from schemas — the standard way to parse API responses, env variables, and form data safely.

children.title: Valibot, ArkType, and Standard Schema
children.description: Zod is the default, but Valibot (smaller bundles) and ArkType (faster) are common alternatives. Standard Schema is a shared interface they all implement, so libraries like tRPC and form tools accept any of them.

children.title: TypeScript project references in monorepos
children.description: Each package in a monorepo gets its own tsconfig with references to its dependencies — tsc --build then handles the correct build order automatically.

children.title: Turborepo + TypeScript
children.description: Turborepo caches TypeScript build outputs across the monorepo — combined with project references, type checking a large monorepo becomes fast.

children.title: tsc --noEmit in CI
children.description: Running tsc --noEmit as a CI step catches type errors without producing output files — faster than a full build and the right gate before merging PRs.

children.title: Type coverage tools
children.description: type-coverage measures what percentage of your code is typed vs any — useful for tracking progress when migrating a JS codebase to TypeScript.

children.title: Publishing libraries with tsdown
children.description: tsdown bundles a library to ESM (and CJS if needed) with declaration files; it replaces tsup, which is no longer actively developed. isolatedDeclarations (TS 5.5) requires explicit export types so .d.ts files can be generated fast and in parallel. Check the result with publint and arethetypeswrong before publishing.

children.title: The native TypeScript compiler
children.description: TypeScript 7 is a rewrite of the compiler in Go (typescript-go, tsgo) and type-checks about 10x faster. TypeScript 6.0 is the bridge release whose deprecations prepare projects for it.

go.title: Go Syntax and Toolchain
go.description: Set up the Go toolchain, understand the module system, and learn core syntax: variables, types, pointers, strings, loops, and functions including closures. Go's simplicity is intentional - the language is small and easy to hold in your head.
topics: go mod init and module structure
Variables, basic types, and zero values
Control flow and range over ints
go.challenge: Build a command-line URL shortener in Go that stores mappings in memory and supports add, lookup, and list commands.

children.title: Simplicity over features
children.description: Go deliberately omits generics (until 1.18), exceptions, and inheritance — forcing explicit, readable code over clever abstractions.

children.title: Compilation model
children.description: Go compiles to a single static binary with no runtime dependencies — fast compilation and trivial deployment are first-class design goals.

children.title: Static typing and zero values
children.description: Every Go variable has a zero value (0, '', false, nil) — no undefined, no null pointer on uninitialized struct fields, which eliminates a whole class of bugs.

children.title: Type inference with :=
children.description: The := short variable declaration infers the type from the right-hand side — reducing verbosity without sacrificing static typing safety.

children.title: Pointers basics
children.description: A pointer holds the address of a value, so a function can change the caller's data instead of a copy. Go has no pointer arithmetic, and the garbage collector manages lifetimes, so pointers are mainly about sharing and avoiding large copies.

children.title: Strings, runes and bytes
children.description: A Go string is a read-only slice of bytes, usually UTF-8. Indexing gives bytes, while ranging over a string decodes runes (Unicode code points). Knowing the difference avoids broken output on non-ASCII text.

resources.label: Go Blog — Strings, bytes, runes and characters
Go by Example — Strings and Runes

children.title: go tool commands
children.description: go build, go run, go test, go fmt, and go vet are all you need for most tasks — one unified tool with no external task runner required.

children.title: gopls language server
children.description: gopls provides autocomplete, go-to-definition, and refactoring in any LSP-compatible editor — install it once and it works everywhere.

children.title: go mod init
children.description: go mod init module/path initializes a module with a go.mod file — the module path is the import path prefix for all packages in the project.

children.title: Standard workspace layout
children.description: Go projects conventionally put cmd/ for executables and internal/ for private packages — internal/ is enforced by the compiler to prevent external imports.

children.title: Closures and variadic functions
children.description: Functions are values in Go: a closure captures variables from its surrounding scope, which is how you build counters, middleware and callbacks. Variadic functions (func f(xs ...int)) accept any number of arguments, like fmt.Println and append.

children.title: Range over ints and per-iteration loop vars
children.description: Since Go 1.22, for i := range 10 loops over integers, and each loop iteration gets its own copy of the loop variable. That fixed a classic bug where goroutines and closures all saw the last value.

resources.label: Go Blog — Fixing For Loops in Go 1.22

go.title: Arrays, Slices, Maps, and Structs
go.description: Master Go's composite types - slices, maps, and structs - and understand the memory model behind them including capacity and append behavior. These types are the foundation of all Go data modeling.

resources.label: A Tour of Go — More types

go.challenge: Refactor the URL shortener to use a struct for the store, add metadata fields (created_at, hit_count), implement a slice-based history log, and use the slices and maps packages to sort and list entries.

children.title: Length vs capacity
children.description: A slice has a pointer, length, and capacity — append grows within capacity without allocation; exceeding it allocates a new backing array and copies.

children.title: Underlying array sharing
children.description: Slicing a slice creates a new header pointing into the same backing array — mutations through one slice affect the other until an append triggers a copy.

children.title: Hash map implementation
children.description: Go maps are hash tables with O(1) average lookup — the zero value of a map is nil (not empty), and writing to a nil map panics.

resources.label: Go Blog — Go maps in action

children.title: Map concurrency
children.description: Go maps are not safe for concurrent reads+writes — use sync.RWMutex or sync.Map when accessing a map from multiple goroutines.

children.title: append patterns
children.description: Common patterns: append(s, x), append(s, other...), and the copy idiom for removing an element — all avoid re-allocating by pre-computing capacity.

children.title: Struct embedding
children.description: Embedding a struct promotes its methods to the outer type — Go's composition mechanism that replaces inheritance without the complexity of class hierarchies.

children.title: slices and maps packages
children.description: The slices and maps standard packages (Go 1.21) provide generic helpers like slices.Sort, slices.Contains, slices.Index and maps.Keys. Prefer them over hand-written loops or the older sort package for everyday slice and map work.

children.title: encoding/json and struct tags
children.description: json:"field_name" tags control JSON key names; omitempty skips zero-value fields — no external library needed for most JSON work.

children.title: Custom marshaling
children.description: Implementing json.Marshaler and json.Unmarshaler interfaces gives full control over JSON serialization for types that don't map cleanly to JSON primitives.

go.title: Interfaces and Methods
go.description: Learn Go's implicit interface satisfaction model, method sets, and how to use interfaces for polymorphism and testability. Go interfaces are small and composable - the standard library demonstrates this with io.Reader and io.Writer.

resources.label: A Tour of Go — Methods and interfaces

go.challenge: Refactor the URL shortener storage behind a Store interface, implement an in-memory and a file-backed version, and swap them at startup via a flag.

children.title: Structural typing in Go
children.description: A type implements an interface by having the right methods — no explicit implements keyword. This decouples interface definitions from implementations across packages.

children.title: Interface internals — nil pitfall
children.description: Interface values are (type, value) pairs — an interface holding a nil pointer is not nil itself. This is the source of the 'nil interface' bug many Go beginners hit.

resources.label: Go FAQ — Why is my nil error value not equal to nil?

children.title: Pointer vs value receivers
children.description: Value receivers work on copies; pointer receivers modify the original. A type's method set with pointer receivers is a superset — you can call pointer methods on addressable values.

children.title: Interface embedding
children.description: Interfaces can embed other interfaces to compose them — io.ReadWriter embeds io.Reader and io.Writer, giving a combined contract in one type.

children.title: io.Reader and io.Writer
children.description: Most Go I/O is built around these two interfaces — any type that reads bytes implements io.Reader, enabling composable pipelines like gzip.NewReader(file).

children.title: fmt.Stringer
children.description: Implementing the Stringer interface (String() string) gives your type a readable representation in fmt.Println — the Go equivalent of toString().

children.title: Small interfaces
children.description: Prefer single-method or two-method interfaces — io.Reader, io.Writer, error. Small interfaces are easier to implement, mock, and compose.

children.title: Mocking with interfaces
children.description: Defining your dependencies as small interfaces lets you swap in test doubles. Hand-written fakes are often enough; when you want generated mocks, use go.uber.org/mock, the maintained fork of the archived golang/mock.

go.title: Error Handling
go.description: Embrace Go's explicit error handling model, define custom error types, and learn idiomatic patterns like wrapping and sentinel errors. Go's approach to errors is deliberate - errors are values, not exceptions.
go.challenge: Add comprehensive error types to the URL shortener (NotFoundError, DuplicateError, ValidationError) with full wrapping, sentinel checks, and user-friendly messages.

children.title: Errors as values
children.description: In Go, errors are just values that implement the error interface — returning them from functions makes error handling explicit at every call site.

children.title: Sentinel errors
children.description: Sentinel errors are package-level error variables (var ErrNotFound = errors.New(...)) that callers compare against — the Go equivalent of typed exception classes.

children.title: fmt.Errorf %w for wrapping
children.description: fmt.Errorf("context: %w", err) wraps an error with context while preserving the original — unwrap the chain with errors.Is or errors.As.

children.title: errors.Is and errors.As
children.description: errors.Is checks if any error in the chain matches a target; errors.As extracts a specific error type from the chain — both unwrap automatically.

children.title: Custom error types
children.description: Implementing the error interface on a struct lets you attach structured data (HTTP status code, field name) that callers can extract with errors.As.

children.title: Panic vs error
children.description: Use errors for expected failure cases; panic for programming errors and invariant violations — recover() catches panics in a deferred function.

children.title: Error handling in HTTP handlers
children.description: A common pattern wraps http.HandlerFunc to return an error, with middleware that maps errors to HTTP status codes — keeping handlers clean.

children.title: errors.Join — Go 1.20
children.description: errors.Join combines multiple errors into one, useful when a function hits several independent failures that should all be reported. errors.Is and errors.As still see every joined error, so callers can check for each one.

go.title: Goroutines and Channels
go.description: Harness Go's concurrency primitives - goroutines and channels - to write concurrent programs that are safe and expressive. Go's CSP model encourages sharing memory by communicating rather than communicating by sharing memory.
go.challenge: Add a concurrent analytics pipeline to the URL shortener that processes click events through a channel and aggregates stats in a background goroutine, and prove it is race-free with go test -race.

children.title: M:N threading model
children.description: Go's scheduler multiplexes M goroutines over N OS threads — thousands of goroutines can run concurrently with minimal overhead compared to OS threads.

children.title: GOMAXPROCS
children.description: GOMAXPROCS controls how many OS threads run Go code at the same time and defaults to the number of CPUs. Since Go 1.25 the default also respects container CPU limits, so you rarely need to set it by hand.

children.title: Buffered vs unbuffered
children.description: Unbuffered channels synchronize sender and receiver; buffered channels decouple them up to the buffer size — choosing correctly avoids deadlocks.

resources.label: The Nature of Channels in Go

children.title: Channel direction in types
children.description: chan<- T (send-only) and <-chan T (receive-only) in function signatures make data flow explicit and prevent misuse at compile time.

children.title: Fan-out and fan-in
children.description: Fan-out distributes work across multiple goroutines; fan-in merges their results through a shared channel — the foundation of Go's pipeline pattern.

children.title: Worker pools
children.description: A fixed-size pool of goroutines reading from a jobs channel limits concurrency and resource usage — the standard pattern for CPU-bound parallel work.

children.title: sync.WaitGroup
children.description: WaitGroup.Add(n) before launching goroutines and Done() in each one lets the main goroutine wait with Wait() — the standard pattern for parallel workloads.

children.title: sync.Mutex
children.description: Mutex protects shared state from concurrent access — Lock() before reading/writing and Unlock() after, ideally deferred to prevent forgetting.

children.title: Race detector (go test -race)
children.description: A data race happens when two goroutines touch the same memory and at least one writes, without synchronization. Running tests and dev builds with -race catches these at runtime; make it a default in CI for any concurrent code.

go.title: The Standard Library
go.description: Explore Go's rich standard library covering HTTP, JSON, file I/O, time, and strings. Go's stdlib is deliberately comprehensive so you can build production-quality programs with minimal external dependencies.
go.challenge: Expose the URL shortener as an HTTP API using only net/http, with JSON request/response bodies, proper status codes, and structured logging.

children.title: Batteries included design
children.description: Go's standard library covers HTTP, JSON, crypto, templating, and testing without external dependencies — reducing supply-chain risk and keeping binaries small.

children.title: Interface-driven design
children.description: The stdlib uses small interfaces (io.Reader, http.Handler, sort.Interface) throughout — your code composes naturally with stdlib by implementing these.

children.title: Handler interface
children.description: http.Handler is just ServeHTTP(ResponseWriter, *Request) — any type implementing it can be mounted on a server, making middleware trivial to compose.

children.title: ServeMux routing
children.description: Go 1.22 added method+path patterns to ServeMux — more expressive routing without external libraries like gorilla/mux.

children.title: context package
children.description: context.Context carries deadlines, cancellations, and request-scoped values across API boundaries — pass it as the first argument to any function that does I/O.

children.title: time package
children.description: time.Duration, time.Now(), and time.After() are the building blocks for timeouts, rate limiting, and scheduled work — all with nanosecond precision.

children.title: Structured logging with log/slog
children.description: log/slog (Go 1.21) writes logs as key-value pairs in text or JSON, with levels and per-request attributes. It is the standard choice for new services and replaces most uses of third-party loggers like zerolog or zap.

resources.label: Go Blog — Structured Logging with slog

children.title: bufio for buffered I/O
children.description: bufio.Scanner and bufio.Writer add buffering to any io.Reader/Writer — critical for line-by-line file reading and reducing syscall overhead.

children.title: io utilities
children.description: io.TeeReader, io.MultiWriter, and io.LimitReader compose readers and writers without copying data — the plumbing of Go's I/O model.

children.title: go:embed
children.description: The //go:embed directive bakes files (HTML templates, SQL migrations, static assets) into the compiled binary at build time. You still ship one file, and the program reads them through an embed.FS like a normal filesystem.

go.title: Testing in Go
go.description: Write table-driven tests, benchmarks, and examples using Go's built-in testing package, and use interfaces for testability. Go's testing tooling is built into the language - no external framework is needed.
go.challenge: Write a full table-driven test suite for the URL shortener including HTTP handler tests using httptest, a fuzz test for the URL parser, benchmarks for the store, and coverage above 85%.

children.title: Table-driven tests
children.description: Table-driven tests define input/expected pairs in a slice and loop — adding a test case is one line, and a failing case names itself via the test name.

children.title: Tests as documentation
children.description: Go test names describe behaviour — TestUserService_CreateUser_ReturnsErrOnDuplicate reads like a spec. Readable test names replace comments.

children.title: testing.B and go test -bench
children.description: Functions starting with Benchmark receive testing.B — run with go test -bench=. to measure nanoseconds per operation and allocations.

resources.label: How to write benchmarks in Go

children.title: pprof profiling
children.description: go test -cpuprofile generates a CPU profile you visualise with go tool pprof — the standard way to identify hot spots before optimising.

children.title: testify/assert
children.description: testify/assert provides expressive assertions (assert.Equal, assert.NoError) that print clear diffs on failure — the most popular Go test helper library.

children.title: httptest package
children.description: httptest.NewRecorder() captures HTTP responses in tests; httptest.NewServer() starts a real test HTTP server — both are in the stdlib with no setup needed.

children.title: Subtests with t.Run
children.description: t.Run(name, func) creates named subtests that can be run selectively with -run — table-driven tests use t.Run to give each case its own name and failure output.

children.title: testdata/ directory
children.description: The testdata/ directory is reserved for test input files and is excluded from builds — the convention for storing JSON fixtures, golden files, and test configs.

children.title: Fuzzing
children.description: Fuzz tests (Go 1.18) feed generated inputs into a function to find crashes and edge cases you would not think to write by hand. They live next to normal tests as FuzzXxx functions and run with go test -fuzz.

children.title: Testing time and concurrency with testing/synctest
children.description: testing/synctest (stable in Go 1.25) runs a test in a bubble with a fake clock, so code that sleeps or uses timeouts finishes instantly and deterministically. It replaces flaky time.Sleep-based tests of concurrent code.

resources.label: Go Blog — Testing concurrent code with testing/synctest

go.title: Go Modules and Dependency Management
go.description: Manage Go module dependencies with go.mod and go.sum, understand versioning semantics, and use popular third-party packages responsibly. The Go module system provides reproducible builds by design.
topics: go get and go mod tidy
go.challenge: Keep routing on the standard library ServeMux and logging on log/slog, then add one real third-party dependency to the URL shortener, pin a developer tool with go get -tool, and keep go.mod and go.sum tidy.

children.title: go.mod and go.sum
children.description: go.mod declares the module path and dependencies; go.sum records cryptographic hashes — both must be committed and go.sum prevents supply-chain attacks.

children.title: Semantic import versioning
children.description: Go requires major version suffixes (/v2) in import paths for v2+ modules — this makes it possible to use multiple major versions simultaneously.

children.title: GOPROXY
children.description: GOPROXY (default: proxy.golang.org) caches module versions — this ensures reproducible builds even if the original source disappears from VCS.

children.title: Module cache
children.description: Downloaded modules are stored in $GOPATH/pkg/mod — go clean -modcache clears it; GOFLAGS=-mod=vendor forces vendor mode.

children.title: go mod tidy
children.description: go mod tidy adds missing and removes unused dependencies from go.mod and go.sum — run it before committing after adding or removing imports.

children.title: go mod vendor
children.description: go mod vendor copies all dependencies into a vendor/ directory — useful for air-gapped builds and ensuring no network access is needed in CI.

children.title: Tool dependencies (go get -tool)
children.description: Since Go 1.24, go.mod can track developer tools (linters, code generators) with go get -tool, and you run them with go tool. This replaces the old tools.go blank-import trick and pins tool versions with the rest of the module.

children.title: GOPRIVATE and private modules
children.description: Set GOPRIVATE (for example GOPRIVATE=github.com/yourorg/*) so the go command fetches those modules directly and skips the public proxy and checksum database. It is the one setting most teams need for internal repositories.

children.title: GOFLAGS for persistent flags
children.description: GOFLAGS sets default flags for all go commands — useful for consistently enabling -mod=vendor or build tags across a project.

go.title: Advanced Go Patterns - Generics, Context, and sync
go.description: Use Go generics (added in 1.18) for reusable data structures, propagate cancellation with context.Context, and synchronize goroutines safely with the sync package. These are the tools of idiomatic production Go.
go.challenge: Add a generic cache layer to the URL shortener with configurable TTL using context for cancellation, and protect concurrent access with sync.RWMutex.

children.title: Type parameters in Go 1.18+
children.description: Go generics use type parameters with constraints — func Map[T, U any](s []T, f func(T) U) []U replaces repetitive slice transformation functions.

children.title: Type constraints
children.description: Constraints are interfaces that restrict which types a type parameter accepts. The built-in comparable allows ==, and the standard cmp.Ordered allows < and >, so you no longer need the experimental x/exp/constraints package.

children.title: Iterators (iter.Seq, range-over-func)
children.description: Since Go 1.23 a for-range loop can range over a function, and iter.Seq[T] is the standard type for such iterators. They let collections and data sources stream values lazily, and slices and maps already return them (slices.Values, maps.Keys).

resources.label: Go Blog — Range Over Function Types

children.title: Context propagation
children.description: Pass context.Context as the first argument through every function that does I/O — this lets callers cancel in-flight operations across goroutine boundaries.

children.title: Context values — use sparingly
children.description: context.WithValue stores request-scoped values (trace IDs, auth tokens) — never use it for required function inputs that belong in the function signature.

children.title: sync.Once
children.description: sync.Once guarantees a function runs exactly once across all goroutines — the standard pattern for lazy initialisation of expensive resources.

children.title: sync.Pool
children.description: sync.Pool recycles temporary objects to reduce GC pressure — used extensively in encoding/json and net/http internally for buffer reuse.

children.title: Functional options pattern
children.description: Accept ...Option variadic arguments to configure a struct — each Option is a function that mutates a config struct, avoiding boolean parameter proliferation.

children.title: sync.Map for concurrent access
children.description: sync.Map is optimised for keys that are written once and read many times, or for goroutines working on disjoint keys. For everything else a plain map guarded by a mutex is clearer and often faster.

go.title: Production Go - Build, Deploy, and Ecosystem
go.description: Build production Go binaries with cross-compilation, profiling, and embed, and understand the broader Go ecosystem for web, CLI, and systems programming. Go's single-binary deployment model is one of its greatest production advantages.

resources.label: 100 Go Mistakes and How to Avoid Them

go.challenge: Package the URL shortener as a cross-compiled binary with embedded static assets, a multi-stage Dockerfile, graceful shutdown, pprof endpoints, and a CI step that runs golangci-lint and govulncheck.

children.title: go build flags
children.description: go build -ldflags='-X main.Version=1.0' injects version info at link time; -trimpath removes local paths from stack traces — both are standard for production binaries.

children.title: CGO_ENABLED=0 for static binaries
children.description: CGO_ENABLED=0 produces a fully static binary with no libc dependency — required for scratch Docker images and Alpine Linux deployments.

children.title: pprof CPU and memory profiling
children.description: go tool pprof visualises CPU and memory profiles from running applications — attach to a live server with net/http/pprof for production profiling.

children.title: Escape analysis
children.description: go build -gcflags='-m' prints which variables escape to the heap — heap allocations are GC pressure; keeping hot data on the stack improves throughput.

children.title: Execution tracing (go tool trace)
children.description: Where pprof shows where time is spent, an execution trace shows when: goroutine scheduling, blocking, GC pauses and latency over time. Since Go 1.22 tracing is cheap enough to leave on in production with the flight recorder.

resources.label: Go Blog — More powerful Go execution traces

children.title: Multi-stage Docker builds
children.description: Build in a FROM golang:1.25 stage, then copy only the binary into a scratch or distroless image. The result is a tiny image with no shell or OS utilities, which shrinks both size and attack surface.

children.title: Cross-compilation
children.description: GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 go build cross-compiles to any platform from any platform — no build server needed for different targets.

children.title: OpenTelemetry for Go
children.description: OpenTelemetry provides standardised tracing and metrics APIs — instrument once and export to Jaeger, Prometheus, or any OTEL-compatible backend.

children.title: Prometheus metrics
children.description: github.com/prometheus/client_golang provides counters, gauges, and histograms — expose them on /metrics and Prometheus scrapes them automatically.

children.title: golangci-lint and staticcheck
children.description: go vet only catches a small set of mistakes. staticcheck adds deeper bug and simplification checks, and golangci-lint runs it plus many other linters in one fast, configurable step that most Go teams wire into CI.

children.title: govulncheck
children.description: govulncheck checks your dependencies against the Go vulnerability database and only reports issues in code your program actually calls. Run it in CI so a vulnerable dependency fails the build before it ships.

resources.label: Tutorial: Find and fix vulnerable dependencies

rust.title: Rust Setup and Basic Syntax
rust.description: Install Rust with rustup, create and run projects with Cargo, and learn the core syntax: variables and mutability, scalar and compound types, the difference between String and &str, and control flow. Understand editions and start every new project on Rust 2024.
rust.challenge: Build a Cargo project with a CLI task manager that can add and list tasks, reading compiler errors carefully to understand Rust's rules from the start.

children.title: Memory safety without GC
children.description: Rust guarantees memory safety at compile time through the ownership system — no garbage collector, no runtime overhead, and no null pointer dereferences or data races by design.

children.title: Zero-cost abstractions
children.description: Rust's iterators, generics, and traits compile to the same machine code as hand-written loops — you pay no runtime cost for the abstraction layer.

children.title: Static typing and type inference
children.description: Rust infers types throughout a function body — you rarely need to annotate locals, but function signatures require explicit types, which serves as documentation.

children.title: Immutability by default
children.description: Variables in Rust are immutable by default — you must explicitly declare mut to allow mutation. This forces deliberate thinking about which data needs to change.

children.title: Scalar and compound types
children.description: Rust has four scalar types (integers, floats, bool, char) and two built-in compound types, tuples and arrays. Integer types are explicit about size and sign, and overflow panics in debug builds, so choosing i32 vs u64 is a real decision.

children.title: String vs &str
children.description: String is an owned, growable, heap-allocated UTF-8 buffer; &str is a borrowed view into UTF-8 bytes stored somewhere else. Functions usually take &str so they accept both, and return String when they create new text. Strings can't be indexed by position because characters vary in byte length.

resources.label: The Rust Book - Storing UTF-8 Text with Strings

children.title: Editions and Rust 2024
children.description: Editions let Rust make small breaking changes without splitting the ecosystem: each crate picks its edition in Cargo.toml and crates of different editions still link together. Rust 2024 is the current edition and the default for cargo new, and cargo fix --edition migrates older code.

resources.label: The Edition Guide - What are editions?

children.title: rustup and toolchain management
children.description: rustup installs and manages Rust toolchains — switch between stable, beta, and nightly per project using a rust-toolchain.toml file.

children.title: Cargo — build system and package manager
children.description: Cargo is Rust's all-in-one tool — cargo new, cargo build, cargo test, cargo run, and cargo publish handle the entire development lifecycle.

children.title: rust-analyzer
children.description: rust-analyzer is the official Rust language server — provides autocomplete, inline type hints, go-to-definition, and refactoring in any LSP-compatible editor.

children.title: Clippy and rustfmt
children.description: clippy is a linter with 600+ idiomatic Rust checks (cargo clippy); rustfmt formats code to the community standard (cargo fmt) — run both in CI.

rust.title: Ownership, Borrowing, and Lifetimes
rust.description: Internalize Rust's ownership system - the most unique and important feature of the language - including moves, borrows, and lifetime annotations. Ownership is what makes Rust memory-safe without a garbage collector.

resources.label: The Rust Book - Validating References with Lifetimes

rust.challenge: Refactor the task manager to pass tasks by reference through helper functions, adding lifetime annotations where necessary and eliminating all unnecessary clones.

children.title: Move semantics by default
children.description: Assigning or passing a value transfers ownership — the original binding is invalidated. This is different from C++ move semantics which are opt-in; in Rust, move is the default.

resources.label: Rust by Example - Ownership and Moves

children.title: Drop and destructor semantics
children.description: When a value goes out of scope, Rust automatically calls drop() — no manual memory management needed, and the Drop trait lets you customize cleanup logic.

children.title: Shared vs exclusive references
children.description: &T is a shared (immutable) reference — many can exist at once. &mut T is an exclusive (mutable) reference — only one can exist at a time. This enforces the aliasing XOR mutation rule at compile time.

children.title: Lifetime annotations
children.description: Lifetimes annotate how long references are valid — the compiler checks that no reference outlives its referent. Most lifetimes are inferred; explicit annotations are only needed when the compiler can't figure it out.

children.title: Clone vs Copy
children.description: Types implementing Copy are duplicated on assignment instead of moved (integers, bools, char) — Clone requires an explicit .clone() call for heap-allocated types like String and Vec.

children.title: Rc and RefCell for shared ownership
children.description: Rc<T> enables multiple owners with reference counting (single-threaded); RefCell<T> moves borrow checking to runtime — use sparingly when the ownership model is genuinely complex.

children.title: Restructuring to satisfy borrows
children.description: Most borrow checker errors are design feedback — splitting a struct, shortening a borrow's scope, or cloning a small value usually resolves them without unsafe.

children.title: The 'static lifetime
children.description: 'static means a reference is valid for the entire program — String literals are 'static. It's often required by thread-spawning APIs since threads may outlive the creating scope.

rust.title: Structs, Enums, and Pattern Matching
rust.description: Model domains using Rust structs and enums, and use pattern matching to exhaustively handle variants. Rust enums are algebraic data types - far more powerful than enums in most languages.

resources.label: The Rust Book - Enums and Pattern Matching

rust.challenge: Refactor the task manager to use a Task enum with variants (Todo, InProgress, Done) each carrying relevant data, and use match everywhere for status transitions.

children.title: Sum types with enum
children.description: Rust enums are algebraic sum types — each variant can hold different data. Option<T> and Result<T,E> are built-in enums that replace null and exceptions respectively.

children.title: Product types with struct
children.description: Structs are product types — they hold all their fields simultaneously. Tuple structs (struct Point(f64, f64)) and unit structs (struct Marker) are lightweight variants.

children.title: Exhaustive matching
children.description: Rust's match must handle every possible variant — the compiler errors if you miss a case. This makes adding new enum variants a safe refactoring: every match site must be updated.

children.title: Destructuring and binding
children.description: Patterns can destructure structs, tuples, and enum variants in place — let (x, y) = point; and if let Ok(value) = result are idiomatic Rust for concise data extraction.

children.title: Option<T> replacing null
children.description: Option<T> is either Some(value) or None — the compiler forces you to handle both cases, making null pointer dereferences impossible in safe Rust.

children.title: Result<T,E> for error handling
children.description: Result<T,E> is either Ok(value) or Err(error) — functions that can fail return Result, and the ? operator propagates errors up the call stack automatically.

children.title: Builder pattern in Rust
children.description: Builder structs with method chaining and a final .build() method are idiomatic Rust for constructing complex types — widely used in libraries like reqwest and tokio.

children.title: Newtype pattern
children.description: Wrapping a primitive in a single-field tuple struct (struct Meters(f64)) creates a distinct type — preventing mixing up values of the same underlying type and enabling custom trait implementations.

rust.title: Collections, Iterators, and Closures
rust.description: Work with the standard collections (Vec, HashMap, HashSet, BTreeMap, VecDeque, BinaryHeap) and pick the right one for the job. Process data with lazy iterator chains and closures, and understand how collect() builds any collection through FromIterator.
topics: Iterator trait and adapters (map, filter, fold)

resources.label: The Rust Book - Iterators and Closures

rust.challenge: Add filtering, sorting, and grouping features to the task manager using iterator adapters, storing tasks in a HashMap keyed by project name.

children.title: Iterator trait and lazy evaluation
children.description: The Iterator trait requires only next() — all other methods (map, filter, take) are provided by default. Iterators are lazy and do nothing until consumed.

children.title: Into and from iterators
children.description: IntoIterator enables for loops on any type; FromIterator enables .collect() — implementing both makes your custom collection work seamlessly with the iterator ecosystem.

children.title: Fn, FnMut, FnOnce
children.description: Closures implement one or more of these traits based on how they capture variables — Fn for shared reference, FnMut for mutable reference, FnOnce for ownership. The compiler infers the right one.

children.title: move closures
children.description: move forces a closure to take ownership of captured variables — required when passing closures to threads that may outlive the creating scope.

children.title: BTreeMap and BTreeSet
children.description: BTreeMap and BTreeSet keep keys sorted, so iteration order is deterministic and range queries are cheap. Reach for them over HashMap when you need ordered output, range lookups, or stable results in tests.

children.title: VecDeque and BinaryHeap
children.description: VecDeque is a ring buffer with fast push and pop at both ends, the natural fit for queues and BFS. BinaryHeap is a max-heap priority queue (wrap items in Reverse for a min-heap), used for schedulers and Dijkstra.

children.title: Chaining iterator adapters
children.description: map, filter, flat_map, take, skip, zip, enumerate — chaining adapters builds a lazy transformation pipeline that compiles to the same code as a hand-written loop.

children.title: collect() into different types
children.description: .collect::<Vec<_>>() materialises an iterator into a Vec; .collect::<HashMap<_,_>>() into a map; .collect::<Result<Vec<_>,_>>() short-circuits on the first error.

children.title: Vec<T>, HashMap<K,V>, HashSet<T>
children.description: Vec is the go-to sequential collection; HashMap provides O(1) average lookup; HashSet tracks unique values — all in std::collections with no external dependencies.

children.title: Entry API for maps
children.description: map.entry(key).or_insert(default) inserts a default value only if the key is absent — avoiding a double lookup compared to checking contains_key then inserting.

rust.title: Traits and Generics
rust.description: Define and implement traits to share behavior across types, and write generic functions and structs constrained by trait bounds. Rust traits are the foundation of zero-cost abstraction.

resources.label: The Rust Book - Generic Types, Traits, and Lifetimes

rust.challenge: Add a generic Storage<T> trait to the task manager with in-memory and file-backed implementations, and a Display impl for pretty-printing all task types.

children.title: Traits as interfaces
children.description: Traits define shared behavior — implementing a trait for a type is explicit and opt-in, unlike structural typing. The orphan rule prevents implementing foreign traits on foreign types.

children.title: Dynamic dispatch with dyn Trait
children.description: Box<dyn Trait> enables runtime polymorphism through a vtable — use it when you need to store heterogeneous types in a collection. The size of dyn Trait objects is known (two pointers).

resources.label: dyn vs impl Trait in Rust

children.title: Static dispatch with impl Trait
children.description: impl Trait in function arguments means the compiler monomorphizes for each concrete type — zero-overhead abstraction with no vtable, but generates separate code per type.

children.title: Where clauses
children.description: where T: Display + Clone is equivalent to the angle bracket syntax but more readable for complex multi-bound generics — required when bounds reference associated types.

children.title: Display, Debug, and From/Into
children.description: Display formats for users ({}); Debug for developers ({:?}). From<T> and Into<T> are reciprocal conversion traits — implement From and you get Into for free.

children.title: PartialEq, Eq, Hash, Ord
children.description: Derive these with #[derive()] for most types — PartialEq enables ==, Hash enables use as HashMap keys, and Ord enables sorting. PartialEq and PartialOrd handle NaN-containing types.

children.title: Extension traits
children.description: Define a trait with new methods and implement it for existing types — adding methods to Vec<T> or &str without modifying the original type, the Rust equivalent of extension methods.

children.title: Associated types vs generics
children.description: Associated types (type Output) bind a single concrete type per implementation; generics allow multiple implementations for the same trait with different type parameters.

rust.title: Error Handling with Result and the ? Operator
rust.description: Write idiomatic Rust error handling using Result<T, E>, the ? operator for propagation, and custom error types. The thiserror and anyhow crates make production error handling ergonomic.
rust.challenge: Add comprehensive error handling to the task manager using thiserror for a library error type and anyhow in main, propagating all I/O errors with context.

children.title: Recoverable vs unrecoverable errors
children.description: Result<T,E> handles recoverable errors (file not found, parse failure); panic! handles unrecoverable programming errors (index out of bounds, logic invariant violation). The distinction drives API design.

children.title: The ? operator desugaring
children.description: expr? desugars to match expr { Ok(v) => v, Err(e) => return Err(e.into()) } — the .into() call converts the error type, enabling ? to work across different error types.

children.title: thiserror for library errors
children.description: thiserror derives the Error trait implementation with #[derive(Error)] and #[error("..")] — the standard for defining custom error types in libraries without boilerplate.

children.title: anyhow for application errors
children.description: anyhow::Result<T> is a boxed error type with context — ideal for application code where you want to propagate any error with additional context rather than defining custom error types.

children.title: Chaining context with anyhow
children.description: .context("failed to read config") wraps an error with a human-readable message — when an error propagates up, each level adds context, producing a readable error chain.

children.title: Converting between error types
children.description: impl From<IoError> for MyError lets ? convert automatically — or use #[from] with thiserror to derive the From implementation.

children.title: std::panic::catch_unwind
children.description: catch_unwind recovers from panics in specific scopes — used in test frameworks and FFI boundaries to prevent panics from crossing into C code.

children.title: unwrap() and expect() in production
children.description: unwrap() panics on None/Err — use expect("descriptive message") instead so panics have context. Reserve both for cases that are genuinely impossible to fail.

rust.title: Modules, Crates, and Cargo Deep Dive
rust.description: Organize Rust code into modules and crates, manage visibility, and use Cargo workspaces for multi-crate projects. Understanding the module system is essential for building maintainable Rust projects.

resources.label: The Rust Book - Packages, Crates, and Modules
The Rust Book - More About Cargo and Crates.io

rust.challenge: Restructure the task manager as a Cargo workspace with a core library crate and a CLI crate, exposing a clean public API from the library.

children.title: Module tree and file layout
children.description: Rust's module tree mirrors the file system — mod foo; in main.rs loads src/foo.rs or src/foo/mod.rs. pub controls visibility at each level of the tree.

children.title: pub(crate) and pub(super)
children.description: pub(crate) makes an item visible within the crate but not to external consumers; pub(super) exposes to the parent module only — fine-grained visibility control without making things fully public.

children.title: Cargo.toml features and optional deps
children.description: Features enable conditional compilation — cargo build --features "async" activates feature-gated code. Optional dependencies become features automatically.

children.title: Workspaces for multi-crate projects
children.description: A Cargo workspace groups multiple crates under one Cargo.lock — shared dependency versions, unified build output, and cross-crate cargo test all in one directory.

children.title: cargo check vs cargo build
children.description: cargo check runs the borrow checker and type checker without producing a binary — 3-5x faster than a full build, ideal for the inner development loop.

children.title: cargo-watch for auto-rebuild
children.description: cargo-watch runs cargo check (or any command) on file save — the Rust equivalent of nodemon, giving instant compiler feedback without manual re-runs.

children.title: docs.rs for crate documentation
children.description: Every crate published to crates.io gets documentation auto-built on docs.rs — the central documentation hub for the entire Rust ecosystem.

children.title: cargo audit for security
children.description: cargo audit checks your dependencies against the RustSec advisory database — run it in CI to catch known vulnerabilities in third-party crates.

rust.title: Lifetimes Advanced and Smart Pointers
rust.description: Go beyond basic lifetimes into advanced scenarios involving structs with references, and learn smart pointers (Box, Rc, RefCell, Arc) for heap allocation and shared ownership. These tools unlock patterns that simple borrowing cannot express.
rust.challenge: Add a shared configuration system to the task manager using Arc<RwLock<Config>> so multiple components can read config concurrently with safe mutation.

children.title: Lifetime elision rules
children.description: The compiler infers lifetimes in most cases using three elision rules — explicit annotations are only needed when the rules don't uniquely determine the output lifetime.

children.title: Variance and subtyping
children.description: In Rust, subtyping only exists between lifetimes: 'a: 'b means 'a outlives 'b, so a longer-lived reference can stand in for a shorter one. Variance decides whether that substitution carries through a type like &'a T, &'a mut T or Cell<T>, which is why some lifetime errors only appear behind mutable references.

resources.label: The Rust Reference - Subtyping and Variance

children.title: Box<T> for heap allocation
children.description: Box<T> allocates T on the heap and owns it — the simplest smart pointer, used for recursive types (where the size is unknown at compile time) and large values.

children.title: Arc<T> and Mutex<T> for shared mutable state
children.description: Arc<T> provides thread-safe reference counting; Mutex<T> provides interior mutability. Arc<Mutex<T>> is the standard pattern for shared mutable state across threads.

children.title: Cow<T> for clone-on-write
children.description: Cow<'a, T> (Clone on Write) holds either a borrowed reference or owned value — avoids cloning when read-only access is sufficient, allocating only when mutation is needed.

children.title: Pin<T> for self-referential types
children.description: Pin<T> prevents a value from being moved in memory — required for async state machines and self-referential structs where internal pointers must remain valid.

children.title: Cell<T> and RefCell<T>
children.description: Cell<T> enables mutation through a shared reference for Copy types; RefCell<T> does the same for non-Copy types with runtime borrow checking — panics instead of compile errors.

children.title: OnceCell and LazyLock
children.description: OnceCell<T> initializes a value exactly once without locking; LazyLock (Rust 1.80+) combines a OnceCell with a lazy initializer — the safe replacement for static mut.

rust.title: Unsafe Rust and FFI
rust.description: Learn exactly what the unsafe keyword allows and how to wrap it in a safe API. You will call C libraries from Rust and expose Rust to other languages, which is how Rust fits into existing systems.
topics: What unsafe permits: raw pointers, unsafe fns, unions
Upholding invariants behind a safe API
Calling C with extern blocks and bindgen
Exposing Rust with extern C and cbindgen
rust.challenge: Write a safe Rust wrapper around a small C library (for example a string or compression API) using bindgen, make it free its memory automatically with Drop, and run the test suite under Miri to show there is no undefined behavior.

children.title: The five unsafe superpowers
children.description: Unsafe code can dereference raw pointers, call unsafe functions, access mutable statics, implement unsafe traits and read union fields. Everything else is still checked by the compiler.

children.title: Safe abstractions over unsafe code
children.description: The goal is a small unsafe block inside a type whose public API cannot be misused. You document the safety invariants and the compiler enforces them for every caller.

children.title: repr(C) and MaybeUninit
children.description: repr(C) gives a struct a predictable C layout, and MaybeUninit lets you hold memory that is not yet initialized without causing undefined behavior.

children.title: Undefined behavior and Miri
children.description: Miri interprets your program and reports invalid pointer use, uninitialized reads and data races that normal tests miss. Run it on every crate that contains unsafe.

children.title: extern blocks and bindgen
children.description: An extern block declares foreign functions, and bindgen generates those declarations from C headers so you do not write them by hand.

children.title: C strings and ownership across the boundary
children.description: CString and CStr convert between Rust and null-terminated C strings. The key rule is that whoever allocated memory must free it, with the matching allocator.

children.title: extern C and no_mangle
children.description: Marking a function extern C and no_mangle gives it a stable symbol name and C calling convention, so C, Python or Go can call it.

children.title: Generating headers with cbindgen
children.description: cbindgen reads your Rust code and writes the matching C header, keeping the two in sync as the API changes.

rust.title: Concurrency and Async Rust
rust.description: Use threads, channels, locks, and atomics to share work safely, with Send and Sync enforced at compile time. Then move to async/await on the Tokio runtime: spawn tasks, wait on several futures with select!, and write async fn directly in traits.
topics: async/await syntax and the Future trait

resources.label: The Rust Book - Async and Await

rust.challenge: Add an async sync feature to the task manager using Tokio that fetches remote task updates from an HTTP endpoint concurrently with local operations.

children.title: Send and Sync traits
children.description: Send means a type can be transferred across thread boundaries; Sync means it can be shared by reference. The compiler enforces these automatically — data races are impossible in safe Rust.

children.title: Fearless concurrency
children.description: The ownership and type system prevent data races at compile time — sharing state between threads requires explicit synchronization (Arc, Mutex, channels), which the type system enforces.

children.title: Future trait and polling
children.description: An async fn compiles to a state machine implementing Future — the executor calls poll() which either returns Poll::Ready(value) or Poll::Pending and registers a waker for re-polling.

children.title: Executors and runtimes
children.description: Rust's async/await requires a runtime to poll Futures — tokio is the dominant choice for production; async-std and smol are lighter alternatives for simpler use cases.

children.title: Atomics and memory ordering
children.description: Atomic types like AtomicUsize and AtomicBool let threads share simple values without a Mutex. Every operation takes an Ordering (Relaxed, Acquire, Release, SeqCst) that controls what other memory writes become visible; SeqCst is the safe default until you can prove a weaker one is correct.

resources.label: Rust Atomics and Locks - Memory Ordering

children.title: async fn in traits
children.description: Since Rust 1.75 you can write async fn directly in a trait, which used to require the async-trait crate and a boxed future. The catch is that the returned future can't be named, so trait objects (dyn Trait) and Send bounds still need extra care.

resources.label: Announcing async fn and return-position impl Trait in traits
The Rust Book - A Closer Look at the Traits for Async

children.title: tokio::spawn and task management
children.description: tokio::spawn launches an async task on the runtime — tasks are lightweight green threads. JoinHandle lets you await the result or cancel the task.

children.title: tokio::select! for concurrent waiting
children.description: select! awaits multiple futures simultaneously and runs the handler for whichever completes first — the idiomatic way to implement timeouts and cancellation in async Rust.

children.title: std::sync::mpsc
children.description: mpsc (multiple producer, single consumer) is Rust's built-in synchronous channel — simple and effective for thread communication without external dependencies.

children.title: tokio channels for async
children.description: tokio provides mpsc, oneshot, broadcast, and watch channels — each optimized for different async communication patterns without blocking the runtime.

rust.title: Macros and Metaprogramming
rust.description: Write code that writes code. You will build declarative macros with macro_rules and procedural macros such as derives, which power much of the Rust ecosystem, including Serde.
topics: Macro hygiene and debugging with cargo expand
Derive macros with syn and quote
Compile-time errors and spans in macros
When to use macros versus generics

resources.label: The Little Book of Rust Macros

rust.challenge: Write a macro_rules macro that builds a HashMap from key-value pairs, then write a derive macro that generates a Builder struct for any struct with named fields, with a clear compile error when used on an enum.

children.title: macro_rules patterns
children.description: A macro_rules macro matches the tokens you give it against patterns and expands to code. Repetitions let one macro handle any number of arguments.

resources.label: The Little Book of Rust Macros

children.title: Hygiene and debugging
children.description: Macro hygiene keeps variables inside a macro from clashing with the caller's. cargo expand shows the generated code so you can see what your macro really produces.

children.title: Macros versus generics
children.description: Reach for a generic function or trait first. Use a macro when you need variable arguments, new syntax or to generate repeated items that functions cannot express.

resources.label: The Little Book of Rust Macros

children.title: Macro maintainability
children.description: Macros are harder to read and to debug than functions. Keep them small, document the accepted syntax and test the expansion with real compile cases.

children.title: Derive macros
children.description: A derive macro receives a struct or enum as a token stream and returns extra code, like an impl block. This is how #[derive(Serialize)] works.

children.title: Attribute and function-like macros
children.description: Attribute macros transform the item they annotate, and function-like macros look like calls. Both run at compile time as separate crates.

children.title: syn and quote
children.description: syn parses Rust tokens into a syntax tree and quote turns tree fragments back into tokens. Together they make procedural macros manageable.

children.title: Good error messages
children.description: Attaching errors to the right span makes a macro feel like part of the language. Return a compile_error with the offending token instead of panicking.

rust.title: Production Rust - Testing, Performance, and Ecosystem
rust.description: Ship Rust with confidence: unit, integration, doc, mock, and property-based tests, Criterion benchmarks and flamegraphs, and structured logging with tracing. Survey the main ecosystem crates (Axum, Clap, Serde) and set up CI and cross-compilation.
topics: Integration tests, doc tests, mocking, and property tests

resources.label: The Rust Book - Writing Automated Tests

rust.challenge: Finalize the task manager with a full test suite, Criterion benchmarks for storage operations, a Clap-powered CLI, and Serde JSON serialization for data persistence.

children.title: #[test] and cargo test
children.description: #[test] marks unit test functions; cargo test discovers and runs them all. Test modules in the same file use #[cfg(test)] to exclude them from production builds.

children.title: Integration tests in tests/
children.description: Files in the tests/ directory are compiled as separate crates — they only access public APIs, making them true integration tests of your library's public interface.

children.title: Mocking and property testing
children.description: mockall generates mock implementations of your traits so you can test code without a real database or network. proptest generates hundreds of random inputs and shrinks any failure to the smallest case, catching edge cases example-based tests miss.

children.title: Criterion for benchmarking
children.description: criterion is the standard Rust benchmarking library — statistical analysis, outlier detection, and HTML reports. Run with cargo bench.

children.title: Profiling with flamegraphs
children.description: cargo-flamegraph generates flamegraphs from perf data — the fastest way to identify which functions consume the most CPU in a Rust program.

children.title: Structured logging with tracing
children.description: tracing records structured events and spans (units of work with a start and end), so logs from concurrent async tasks stay connected. tracing-subscriber decides where they go and in what format; it is the standard choice over the older log crate for services.

children.title: rustdoc and doc tests
children.description: Code examples in /// doc comments are compiled and run by cargo test, so documentation can't silently drift out of date. cargo doc renders the same comments into the HTML you see on docs.rs.

children.title: Axum and Actix-web
children.description: Axum (from the Tokio team) uses tower middleware and type-safe extractors; Actix-web is battle-tested and fastest in benchmarks — both are production-ready async web frameworks.

children.title: Serde for serialization
children.description: serde is the universal Rust serialization framework — #[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)] handles JSON, TOML, YAML, MessagePack, and dozens of other formats with zero boilerplate.

children.title: GitHub Actions for Rust
children.description: A standard Rust CI workflow runs cargo test, cargo clippy -- -D warnings, and cargo fmt --check — catching logic bugs, lint warnings, and formatting issues on every PR.

children.title: Cross-compilation with cross
children.description: cross is a wrapper around cargo that uses Docker to cross-compile for any target — essential for building Linux ARM binaries from macOS/Windows or targeting embedded platforms.

java.title: Java Syntax and JVM Basics
java.description: Set up the JDK, understand the Java compilation model and the JVM, and learn core syntax: variables, primitives, strings, arrays, control flow and methods. Since Java 25 a first program can be a compact source file with an instance main method, so you can start small and add classes as the program grows.
topics: Compact source files and instance main (Java 25)
java.challenge: Build a command-line bank account simulator in Java with deposit, withdraw, and balance commands as a Maven or Gradle project.

children.title: Bytecode and class loading
children.description: Java compiles to platform-independent bytecode (.class files) that the JVM interprets or JIT-compiles — the class loader finds and loads classes on demand at runtime.

children.title: JIT compilation
children.description: The JVM profiles running code and JIT-compiles hot methods to native machine code — this is why Java warms up slowly but reaches near-native speed for long-running processes.

children.title: Primitive vs reference types
children.description: Java has 8 primitive types (int, long, double, boolean, etc.) stored by value, and reference types (objects) stored as heap pointers — autoboxing converts between them automatically but adds overhead.

children.title: Strings, arrays and type casting
children.description: Strings are immutable objects, so build them in loops with StringBuilder and compare them with equals(), never ==. Arrays have a fixed length set at creation. Widening casts (int to long) are automatic, while narrowing casts (double to int) need an explicit cast and can silently lose data.

children.title: JDK installation and JAVA_HOME
children.description: Install a JDK (not just JRE) and set JAVA_HOME — use SDKMAN! to manage multiple JDK versions per project, like nvm for Java.

children.title: IDE setup — IntelliJ IDEA
children.description: IntelliJ IDEA is the industry-standard Java IDE — its refactoring tools, debugger, and code analysis are unmatched. The community edition is free and sufficient for learning.

children.title: Maven project structure
children.description: Maven's standard layout (src/main/java, src/test/java) and pom.xml are understood by every Java tool — start with mvn archetype:generate for a working skeleton.

children.title: Gradle as an alternative
children.description: Gradle uses Groovy/Kotlin DSL instead of XML — faster incremental builds than Maven and the build system of choice for Android and many modern Java projects.

java.title: Object-Oriented Programming in Java
java.description: Master Java OOP fundamentals: classes, inheritance, polymorphism and encapsulation, plus the other class shapes you meet every day: enums, nested classes and records. Builder and Singleton live in the design patterns layer.
java.challenge: Refactor the bank simulator into an OOP design with Account, SavingsAccount, and CheckingAccount classes using inheritance and polymorphic transaction handling. Model the account status with an enum and the account summary with a record.

children.title: Encapsulation and access modifiers
children.description: private, protected, package-private, and public control visibility — encapsulation hides implementation details so internal changes don't break callers.

children.title: Inheritance vs composition
children.description: Java supports single class inheritance but multiple interface implementation — prefer composition (has-a) over deep inheritance (is-a) to avoid fragile base class problems.

children.title: Dynamic dispatch
children.description: Java uses virtual dispatch for all non-static, non-final, non-private methods — the JVM calls the method on the actual runtime type, not the declared type.

children.title: Abstract classes vs interfaces
children.description: Abstract classes share implementation across related classes; interfaces define contracts for unrelated classes. Since Java 8, interfaces can have default methods, blurring the line.

resources.label: When to use abstract class vs interface

children.title: Enums
children.description: An enum is a class with a fixed set of instances, so it can have fields, constructors and methods, not just names. Use one whenever a value comes from a closed set (status, direction, plan). switch over an enum is checked by the compiler, and EnumMap and EnumSet are fast built-in collections for them.

children.title: Nested and inner classes
children.description: A static nested class is just a class scoped inside another, while an inner (non-static) class holds a hidden reference to its outer instance. Prefer static nested classes unless you need that reference, because the hidden pointer can keep large objects alive. Anonymous classes are mostly replaced by lambdas today.

children.title: @Data, @Builder, @Value
children.description: Lombok generates boilerplate (getters, setters, equals, hashCode, toString) at compile time — widely used in production Java to reduce noise.

children.title: Records (Java 16+)
children.description: Records are immutable data carriers with auto-generated constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode, and toString — the modern Java replacement for many Lombok uses.

java.title: Collections Framework and Generics
java.description: Use the Java Collections Framework effectively (List, Set, Map, Queue, and the Java 21 sequenced collection interfaces) and write generic classes and methods for type-safe reusable code. The collections framework is one of Java's most-used APIs.
topics: Generic type parameters and type erasure
java.challenge: Add a transaction history using a LinkedList and a sorted index using TreeMap to the bank simulator, with generic utility methods for balance calculations.

children.title: ArrayList vs LinkedList
children.description: ArrayList is backed by an array — O(1) random access, O(n) insert/delete. LinkedList is a doubly-linked list — O(1) insert at ends but poor cache locality. ArrayList wins for most use cases.

children.title: HashMap internals
children.description: HashMap uses an array of buckets with chaining for collisions — Java 8+ converts buckets to balanced trees when they exceed 8 entries, preventing O(n) worst-case lookups.

children.title: Type erasure
children.description: Java generics are erased at runtime — List<String> and List<Integer> are both just List at the bytecode level. This preserves binary compatibility but prevents runtime type checks.

children.title: Wildcards and bounds
children.description: ? extends T (upper bound, read-only) and ? super T (lower bound, write-only) enable flexible generic APIs — the PECS principle (Producer Extends, Consumer Super) guides usage.

children.title: Choosing the right collection
children.description: List for ordered sequences, Set for uniqueness, Map for key-value lookups, Queue/Deque for FIFO/LIFO — knowing the interface keeps code flexible.

children.title: Collections utility methods
children.description: Collections.sort(), Collections.unmodifiableList(), Collections.synchronizedList() — the Collections class provides algorithms and wrapper factories for all collection types.

children.title: List.of() and Map.of()
children.description: Java 9+ factory methods create truly unmodifiable collections — they throw UnsupportedOperationException on mutation and are more memory-efficient than wrapped mutable collections.

children.title: Sequenced collections (Java 21)
children.description: SequencedCollection, SequencedSet and SequencedMap give every ordered collection the same getFirst(), getLast(), addFirst() and reversed() methods. Before Java 21, getting the last element meant list.get(list.size() - 1) or iterating a LinkedHashSet to the end.

java.title: Exception Handling and File I/O
java.description: Handle exceptions correctly using checked and unchecked exception hierarchies, read and write files with the NIO.2 API, and use the core APIs every real program needs: java.time for dates and the built-in HttpClient for calling web services.
java.challenge: Add persistent account storage to the bank simulator using java.nio.file and JSON serialization, with custom exceptions for insufficient funds and invalid accounts. Timestamp every transaction with java.time and fetch a currency exchange rate with HttpClient.

children.title: Checked vs unchecked exceptions
children.description: Checked exceptions (extend Exception) must be caught or declared — they model recoverable conditions. Unchecked (extend RuntimeException) indicate programming errors and don't require handling.

children.title: Exception chaining
children.description: Passing the cause to a new exception (throw new ServiceException("msg", e)) preserves the original stack trace — essential for debugging production errors without losing context.

children.title: Custom exception classes
children.description: Creating domain-specific exceptions (OrderNotFoundException extends RuntimeException) makes error handling more expressive and lets callers catch specific failure modes.

children.title: NIO.2 vs old IO
children.description: java.nio.file (NIO.2, Java 7+) replaced java.io.File — Path, Files, and StandardOpenOption are the modern API with better error messages and atomic operations.

children.title: try-with-resources
children.description: try(Resource r = new Resource()) automatically calls r.close() on exit — any class implementing AutoCloseable works, eliminating finally blocks for resource cleanup.

children.title: Files utility class
children.description: Files.readAllLines(), Files.write(), Files.walk() — the static utility methods on Files cover most file operations in one or two lines without manual stream management.

children.title: Date and time with java.time
children.description: java.time (Java 8+) replaced the mutable, error-prone Date and Calendar classes. Use Instant for machine timestamps, LocalDate/LocalDateTime for calendar values without a zone, and ZonedDateTime when the time zone matters. All types are immutable and thread-safe.

children.title: HTTP client (java.net.http)
children.description: Since Java 11 the JDK ships an HttpClient that supports HTTP/2, sync send() and async sendAsync() calls. It removes the need for HttpURLConnection or a third-party library for simple API calls, and it works well with virtual threads.

java.title: Streams API and Lambdas
java.description: Transform, filter, and aggregate data using lambdas and the Streams API. Streams are the idiomatic way to process collections in modern Java: Stream.toList() (Java 16) shortens the most common pipeline, and stream gatherers (Java 24) add custom intermediate operations.
topics: Lambda expression syntax and method references
java.challenge: Rewrite all account querying and reporting logic in the bank simulator using Streams, grouping transactions by type using Collectors.groupingBy.

children.title: Function, Predicate, Consumer, Supplier
children.description: java.util.function defines the standard functional interface vocabulary — Function<T,R> maps, Predicate<T> tests, Consumer<T> processes, Supplier<T> produces.

children.title: Method references
children.description: Method references (ClassName::method) are a shorthand for lambdas that just call a method — cleaner and more readable when the lambda body is a single method call.

children.title: Lazy evaluation
children.description: Stream operations are lazy — intermediate operations (filter, map) are not executed until a terminal operation (collect, forEach) is called. This enables short-circuit optimization.

children.title: Parallel streams
children.description: stream().parallel() distributes work across the ForkJoinPool — beneficial for CPU-bound operations on large collections, but adds overhead for small or I/O-bound work.

children.title: collect() and Collectors
children.description: Collectors.groupingBy(), joining() and toMap() cover most terminal aggregations. For a plain list, Stream.toList() (Java 16+) is shorter than collect(Collectors.toList()) and returns an unmodifiable list. When no built-in intermediate operation fits, Java 24 gatherers (Gatherers.windowFixed, fold) let you write your own.

children.title: flatMap for nested collections
children.description: flatMap flattens a stream of collections into a single stream — essential for processing nested data structures like lists of lists.

children.title: Stream vs for loop
children.description: Streams are more declarative and composable; for loops are more performant for simple operations — prefer streams for readability unless profiling shows a bottleneck.

children.title: Optional with streams
children.description: Optional.stream() (Java 9+) converts an Optional to a 0-or-1 element stream — enables flatMapping optionals inside stream pipelines cleanly.

java.title: Concurrency and Multithreading
java.description: Write concurrent Java programs using threads, the Executor framework, concurrent collections and locks, then move to the modern model: virtual threads for cheap blocking I/O, plus structured concurrency and scoped values for managing groups of tasks safely.
java.challenge: Add concurrent transaction processing to the bank simulator using an executor with one virtual thread per task, protecting balance state with appropriate synchronization primitives. Process a batch of transfers with StructuredTaskScope so one failure cancels the rest.

children.title: Structured concurrency and scoped values
children.description: StructuredTaskScope treats a group of subtasks as one unit: if one fails the others are cancelled and no thread leaks past the block (still a preview in Java 25). ScopedValue, final in Java 25, shares immutable context like the current user with child threads and is the modern replacement for ThreadLocal.

children.title: synchronized and volatile
children.description: synchronized provides mutual exclusion and visibility; volatile provides visibility only — using volatile for a read-modify-write (i++) is still a data race.

children.title: Virtual threads
children.description: Virtual threads (Java 21) are cheap JVM-managed threads, so you can run one per request and write plain blocking code instead of async callbacks. Since Java 24 they no longer pin their carrier thread inside synchronized blocks. Use them for I/O-bound work, not to speed up CPU-bound loops, and never pool them.

resources.label: JEP 491 — Synchronize Virtual Threads without Pinning

children.title: Deadlock detection
children.description: Deadlocks occur when two threads each hold a lock the other needs — thread dumps (kill -3 or jstack) reveal deadlocked threads with their lock acquisition chains.

children.title: ExecutorService and thread pools
children.description: ExecutorService manages a pool of threads for task submission — Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n) and newCachedThreadPool() cover most use cases without managing threads manually.

children.title: CompletableFuture
children.description: CompletableFuture enables async pipelines with thenApply, thenCompose, and thenCombine — the modern Java replacement for raw Future that supports non-blocking composition.

children.title: AtomicInteger and AtomicReference
children.description: java.util.concurrent.atomic classes provide lock-free thread-safe operations using CAS (compare-and-swap) — faster than synchronized for simple counters and flags.

children.title: ReentrantLock
children.description: ReentrantLock provides more flexibility than synchronized — tryLock(), lockInterruptibly(), and fairness policy give you control over lock acquisition that synchronized doesn't.

java.title: Design Patterns in Java
java.description: Apply classic Gang of Four design patterns in Java - singleton, builder, factory, observer, and strategy - and understand when each applies. Design patterns are the shared vocabulary of Java software architecture.
java.challenge: Refactor the bank simulator using the Builder pattern for account creation, Strategy for transaction fee calculation, and Observer for balance change notifications.

children.title: Single Responsibility and Open/Closed
children.description: SRP — a class should have one reason to change. OCP — open for extension, closed for modification. These two principles drive most refactoring decisions in Java codebases.

children.title: Dependency Inversion
children.description: High-level modules should depend on abstractions (interfaces), not concrete classes — this is the foundation of testable, loosely-coupled Java architecture.

children.title: Strategy pattern
children.description: Strategy encapsulates interchangeable algorithms behind an interface — swapping implementations at runtime without if/else chains is its main purpose.

children.title: Observer pattern
children.description: Observer decouples event producers from consumers — Java's built-in PropertyChangeListener and modern reactive frameworks (RxJava, Spring Events) are both Observer implementations.

children.title: Factory Method and Abstract Factory
children.description: Factory Method delegates instantiation to subclasses; Abstract Factory creates families of related objects — both decouple callers from concrete classes.

children.title: Annotations and dependency injection
children.description: Annotations like @Override or @Inject are metadata that the compiler, tools or frameworks read. Dependency injection frameworks such as Spring use them to build objects and hand each one its dependencies, so classes ask for interfaces in their constructor instead of creating concrete classes themselves.

children.title: Decorator pattern
children.description: Decorator wraps an object to add behaviour dynamically — Java's I/O streams (BufferedInputStream wrapping FileInputStream) are the classic real-world example.

children.title: Proxy and AOP
children.description: Proxy wraps an object to control access — Spring's @Transactional and @Cacheable use dynamic proxies under the hood to add cross-cutting concerns transparently.

java.title: Modern Java - Records, Sealed Classes, and Pattern Matching
java.description: Adopt modern Java features from Java 14-25 including records, sealed classes, text blocks, pattern matching for switch, record patterns and unnamed variables, and the Java 25 additions that make small programs simpler: compact source files and module imports. Modern Java is far more expressive than the Java 8 many developers learned.
topics: Pattern matching for instanceof and switch
