Module imports and compact source files (Java 25)
java.challenge: Refactor transaction types in the bank simulator to sealed interfaces with record implementations, using pattern matching switch for all transaction dispatch logic.

children.title: Records internals
children.description: Records are final classes with auto-generated canonical constructor, accessors (not getters), equals, hashCode, and toString — the compiler enforces immutability by making fields final.

children.title: Sealed classes
children.description: Sealed classes restrict which classes can extend or implement them — combined with pattern matching, they enable exhaustive switch expressions over type hierarchies.

children.title: Pattern matching for instanceof
children.description: if (obj instanceof String s) eliminates the explicit cast after an instanceof check — the pattern variable s is in scope only in the true branch.

children.title: Switch expressions and pattern matching
children.description: Java 21 switch can match on types, guarded patterns, and deconstruct records — enabling exhaustive handling of sealed type hierarchies without manual casting.

children.title: Text blocks
children.description: Text blocks (Java 15+) are multi-line string literals with automatic indentation trimming — essential for embedding JSON, SQL, and HTML without escape hell.

children.title: var — local type inference
children.description: var infers the variable type from the initializer (Java 10+) — use it to reduce verbosity for long generic types, but keep it where the type is obvious from context.

children.title: Record patterns and unnamed variables
children.description: Record patterns deconstruct a record right in a switch or instanceof (case Point(int x, int y)), and nest for deeper data. The unnamed variable _ (Java 22) marks a binding you do not use, so patterns and catch blocks stay readable and the compiler knows the value is ignored.

children.title: Module imports and compact source files
children.description: Java 25 lets a small program skip the class declaration and write void main() directly in a compact source file, with IO.println for console output. import module java.base; brings in every package a module exports with one line. Both lower the ceremony for scripts and learning without changing how large apps are built.

resources.label: JEP 512 — Compact Source Files and Instance Main Methods

java.title: Testing with JUnit and Mockito
java.description: Write unit and integration tests with JUnit Jupiter, including parameterized and nested tests, mock dependencies with Mockito, and test HTTP APIs end to end with REST Assured. Testing is a first-class practice in Java, and its ecosystem is among the best in any language.
java.challenge: Write a complete JUnit test suite for the bank simulator with Mockito mocks for external storage, parameterized tests for edge cases, REST Assured tests for its HTTP endpoints, and JaCoCo coverage above 80%.

children.title: JUnit 5 architecture
children.description: JUnit 5 is split into JUnit Platform (launcher), JUnit Jupiter (API), and JUnit Vintage (legacy runner) — this separation enables multiple testing frameworks on one platform.

children.title: Test lifecycle annotations
children.description: @BeforeEach, @AfterEach, @BeforeAll, @AfterAll manage test setup and teardown — @BeforeAll and @AfterAll require static methods unless the test class is @TestInstance(PER_CLASS).

children.title: How Mockito generates mocks
children.description: Mockito uses bytecode generation (via ByteBuddy or cglib) to create subclass-based mocks at runtime — this is why you can't mock final classes without the MockMaker extension.

children.title: Argument matchers
children.description: any(), eq(), argThat() let you match method arguments flexibly in when() and verify() — mixing matchers and raw values requires wrapping all args in matchers.

children.title: Given-When-Then structure
children.description: Organizing tests into Given (setup), When (action), Then (assertion) sections makes tests self-documenting and maps directly to BDD-style specifications.

children.title: Parameterized tests
children.description: @ParameterizedTest with @ValueSource, @CsvSource, or @MethodSource runs the same test logic with multiple inputs — replacing copy-pasted test methods.

children.title: Spring Boot Test slice annotations
children.description: @WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest, @JsonTest load only the relevant slice of the Spring context — faster than @SpringBootTest for focused integration tests.

children.title: Testcontainers
children.description: Testcontainers starts real Docker containers (Postgres, Redis, Kafka) for integration tests — eliminating in-memory database mismatch bugs.

java.title: JVM Internals: Memory Model, Garbage Collection, and JIT
java.description: Understand what the JVM does with your code. You will learn class loading, the heap and stack, how the garbage collectors differ, how the JIT compiler optimizes hot code, and the Java Memory Model that makes concurrent code correct.
topics: Heap, stack, metaspace and object layout
Garbage collectors: G1 and generational ZGC
The Java Memory Model and happens-before
Measuring with JMH and Java Flight Recorder
java.challenge: Write a small allocation-heavy program, run it under two different garbage collectors with GC logging enabled, and explain the pause times you see. Then write a JMH benchmark showing the effect of JIT warm-up and one inlining decision.

children.title: Heap, stack and metaspace
children.description: Objects live on the heap, each thread has its own stack, and class metadata lives in metaspace. Knowing which one is full tells you which error you are looking at.

children.title: Class loading
children.description: The JVM loads classes lazily through class loaders, then links and initializes them. This explains static initialization order and most ClassNotFound errors.

children.title: How the collectors differ
children.description: G1 (the default) balances throughput and pause time in regions, ZGC targets very short pauses on large heaps, and Parallel favors raw throughput. ZGC is generational by default since Java 23, so it now collects short-lived objects cheaply too. Pick by latency requirement, not habit.

resources.label: JEP 474 — ZGC: Generational Mode by Default

children.title: Reading GC logs
children.description: Unified logging with -Xlog:gc shows how often collections run and how long they pause. Learn to tell a memory leak from a simple undersized heap.

children.title: Tiered compilation
children.description: The JVM starts by interpreting, then compiles hot methods with C1 and finally C2. This is why a benchmark's first runs are slower than later ones.

children.title: Inlining and escape analysis
children.description: The JIT inlines small methods and can avoid allocating objects that never escape a method. Both make clean, small methods cheaper than they look.

children.title: The Java Memory Model
children.description: The memory model defines when one thread's write is guaranteed to be visible to another. happens-before edges from volatile, synchronized and final fields are what make code correct.

children.title: JMH and Flight Recorder
children.description: JMH handles warm-up, forking and dead-code elimination so microbenchmarks are trustworthy, and Flight Recorder profiles a running application with low overhead.

java.title: Production Java - Build Tools, Performance, and Ecosystem
java.description: Ship production Java with Maven or Gradle, add structured logging with SLF4J and Logback, profile with JFR and async-profiler, and talk to a database through JDBC and Spring Boot. Java's mature ecosystem means there is a well-tested library for nearly every problem.
topics: Profiling with Java Flight Recorder and async-profiler
JDBC and data access with Spring Boot
GraalVM native image and Docker packaging
java.challenge: Package the bank simulator as a fat JAR with Maven, move account storage to a SQL database through JDBC, replace System.out with SLF4J logging, and profile it with JFR under simulated load. Add a Spring Boot HTTP layer as a bonus extension.

children.title: Maven lifecycle and plugins
children.description: Maven's build lifecycle (validate, compile, test, package, install, deploy) runs plugins in order — understanding phases lets you hook custom tasks at the right point.

children.title: Gradle incremental builds
children.description: Gradle tracks task inputs and outputs — if nothing changed, tasks are UP-TO-DATE and skipped. Build caching shares results across machines, making CI dramatically faster.

children.title: Logging with SLF4J and Logback
children.description: SLF4J is the logging API your code calls and Logback (Spring Boot's default) is the implementation behind it, so libraries never force a logging backend on you. Use parameterized messages (log.info("id={}", id)) instead of string concatenation, and log levels instead of System.out.

children.title: JVM profiling with async-profiler
children.description: async-profiler samples CPU and allocations with low overhead — the go-to tool for finding hot methods and memory pressure in production JVM applications.

children.title: Spring Boot
children.description: Spring Boot is the de-facto Java backend framework — auto-configuration, embedded servers, and production-ready starters let you ship REST APIs without XML configuration.

children.title: JDBC and data access
children.description: JDBC is the standard API every Java database library builds on: a connection, a PreparedStatement with ? parameters (which prevents SQL injection) and a ResultSet. In Spring Boot you rarely open connections yourself; a HikariCP pool and JdbcClient or Spring Data handle it.

children.title: GitHub Actions for Java
children.description: A Maven or Gradle workflow with actions/setup-java handles JDK installation, caching, and parallel matrix builds across multiple Java versions in CI.

children.title: Docker for Java apps
children.description: Multi-stage Docker builds compile with a JDK image and run with a JRE image — use distroless or Eclipse Temurin JRE images to minimize attack surface and image size.

cpp.title: C++ Syntax and Compilation Model
cpp.description: Set up a C++ compiler (GCC or Clang), understand the preprocessing, compilation, and linking pipeline, and learn basic modern syntax: auto, the named C++ casts, and type-safe output with std::format and std::print. C++ is a compiled systems language where understanding the build model is as important as the syntax.
cpp.challenge: Build a command-line contact book in C++ with add, search, and list commands, compiled with CMake and organized into header and source files.

children.title: Preprocessing, compiling, linking
children.description: C++ source goes through three phases: the preprocessor expands macros and includes, the compiler produces object files, and the linker combines them into an executable.

children.title: Translation units
children.description: Each .cpp file is a separate translation unit compiled independently — this is why you include headers (declarations) not other .cpp files (definitions).

children.title: C++ additions over C
children.description: C++ adds classes, templates, references, operator overloading, exceptions, and the STL on top of C — understanding C first makes C++ semantics clearer.

children.title: std::print and std::format
children.description: std::format (C++20) builds strings with Python-style {} placeholders that are type-checked at compile time, and std::print (C++23) writes them straight to the console. They replace both printf, which is not type-safe, and long chains of iostream << operators.

children.title: g++ flags
children.description: Key flags: -std=c++20, -O2 (optimize), -Wall -Wextra (warnings), -g (debug info) — always compile with warnings enabled and treat them as errors in production.

children.title: CMake basics
children.description: CMake is the de-facto build system for C++ — cmake_minimum_required, project(), add_executable(), and target_compile_features() cover most project setups.

children.title: VS Code + clangd
children.description: clangd provides C++-aware autocomplete, diagnostics, and go-to-definition — it reads compile_commands.json generated by CMake for accurate project-wide analysis.

children.title: auto and C++ casts
children.description: auto lets the compiler deduce a variable's type from its initializer, which keeps long iterator and template types out of your code. When you must convert types, use static_cast and friends instead of C-style casts: they say what kind of conversion you mean and are easy to search for.

cpp.title: Pointers, References, and Memory Management
cpp.description: Understand pointers and references, manual memory management with new and delete, and why unmanaged memory is dangerous. This layer is where C++ diverges most sharply from other modern languages.

resources.label: LearnCpp - Dynamic memory with new and delete

cpp.challenge: Rewrite the contact book using raw pointers for dynamic storage, then intentionally introduce and diagnose a memory leak using Valgrind.

children.title: Stack vs heap
children.description: Local variables live on the stack and are automatically destroyed when they go out of scope; heap allocations with new persist until delete — mismanaging them causes leaks.

children.title: Pointer arithmetic
children.description: Incrementing a pointer moves it by sizeof(T) bytes — this is how array indexing works under the hood, and why pointer+offset is equivalent to array subscript.

children.title: Dangling pointers and use-after-free
children.description: Using a pointer after the object it pointed to was destroyed is undefined behaviour — the program may appear to work, crash, or be exploited silently.

children.title: UB and compiler optimizations
children.description: Compilers assume UB never happens and optimize accordingly — this can silently remove safety checks. -fsanitize=address catches many UB cases at runtime.

resources.label: What Every C Programmer Should Know About UB

children.title: Valgrind memcheck
children.description: Valgrind detects heap corruption, use-after-free, and memory leaks at runtime — run with valgrind --leak-check=full on any program handling dynamic memory.

children.title: AddressSanitizer
children.description: ASan is a fast compiler-based sanitizer (compile with -fsanitize=address) that detects buffer overflows and use-after-free with minimal overhead.

children.title: RAII intro
children.description: Wrapping a resource (file, mutex, connection) in a class whose destructor releases it guarantees cleanup even on exceptions — the core C++ resource management pattern.

children.title: Object lifetime and storage duration
children.description: Every object has a storage duration (automatic, static, thread or dynamic) that decides when its memory exists, and a lifetime that starts when construction finishes and ends at destruction. Most pointer bugs are accesses outside an object's lifetime, so knowing these rules tells you exactly when a pointer or reference becomes invalid.

cpp.title: Classes, OOP, and RAII
cpp.description: Define C++ classes with constructors, destructors, and operator overloading, use inheritance and virtual dispatch, and learn the class-design rules that keep resource handling correct: the Rule of Zero, Three and Five, move-only types, and the Pimpl idiom.
topics: Rule of Zero, Three and Five

resources.label: C++ Core Guidelines - Classes and class hierarchies

cpp.challenge: Refactor the contact book into a RAII-safe class design where the ContactBook destructor releases all memory, with copy and move constructors implemented correctly.

children.title: Pimpl idiom
children.description: Pimpl (pointer to implementation) moves a class's private members into a separate struct held by a std::unique_ptr. Changing the implementation then no longer forces every file that includes the header to recompile, and it keeps a library's binary interface stable.

children.title: Multiple and diamond inheritance
children.description: A class can inherit from several bases, but if two of them share a common base you get two copies of it (the diamond problem). Virtual inheritance keeps a single shared copy at some cost in complexity, which is why most designs keep multiple inheritance to interface-only bases.

children.title: vtable mechanism
children.description: Virtual functions are dispatched through a vtable — a per-class array of function pointers. Each virtual call is a two-pointer dereference, which is why virtual dispatch has a (small) cost.

children.title: Virtual destructor
children.description: Always declare destructors virtual in base classes — without it, deleting a derived class through a base pointer calls only the base destructor, leaking the derived part.

children.title: Pure virtual interfaces
children.description: A class with only pure virtual methods (= 0) is an abstract interface — the standard C++ way to define a contract without any implementation.

children.title: Composition over inheritance
children.description: Deep inheritance hierarchies are fragile in C++ — prefer composing objects and using interfaces over long inheritance chains.

children.title: Rule of zero, three and five
children.description: If a class manages a resource and needs a custom destructor, it almost always needs custom copy operations too (Rule of Three), plus move operations for efficiency (Rule of Five). The better default is the Rule of Zero: hold resources in members like std::vector or std::unique_ptr and write none of these functions yourself.

children.title: Non-copyable and move-only types
children.description: Some objects, like a file handle or a mutex owner, must never be duplicated. Mark the copy constructor and copy assignment as = delete so the compiler rejects copies, and provide move operations if ownership should be transferable, as std::unique_ptr does.

cpp.title: Move Semantics and Value Categories
cpp.description: Understand lvalues, rvalues and xvalues, and how rvalue references let an object hand over its resources instead of copying them. Move semantics is why modern containers and smart pointers are cheap to pass around, and getting it wrong silently turns moves back into copies.
topics: Copy elision and return value optimization
The Rule of Zero and the Rule of Five revisited

resources.label: LearnCpp - Move constructors and move assignment

cpp.challenge: Write a move-only Buffer class that owns a heap array and implement the Rule of Five by hand. Add copy and move counters, then prove that a std::vector<Buffer> reallocation moves its elements, and show what changes when the move constructor is not noexcept.

children.title: lvalue, prvalue and xvalue
children.description: Every expression has a value category that decides whether it can be moved from. An lvalue has an identity you can name, a prvalue is a temporary, and an xvalue is an object whose resources may be taken.

children.title: Rvalue references
children.description: T&& binds to temporaries and lets a function know the argument will not be used again. A named rvalue reference is itself an lvalue, which is the source of most move bugs.

children.title: std::move is a cast
children.description: std::move does not move anything: it casts its argument to an rvalue so a move constructor or assignment can be chosen. After a move the source stays valid but unspecified.

children.title: Move constructor and assignment
children.description: A move constructor steals the resources of the source and leaves it in a safe empty state. Implement move assignment to release the current resources and handle self-assignment.

children.title: Copy elision and RVO
children.description: Returning a local or temporary by value usually constructs it directly in the caller, with no copy and no move. Writing return std::move(local) disables this and is a common mistake.

children.title: noexcept moves and std::vector
children.description: std::vector only moves its elements on reallocation if the move constructor is noexcept; otherwise it copies to keep its strong exception guarantee. Mark moves noexcept whenever they cannot throw.

children.title: Forwarding references
children.description: In a deduced context, T&& can bind to both lvalues and rvalues. It is a forwarding reference, not an rvalue reference, and it is the basis of generic wrapper functions.

children.title: std::forward and perfect forwarding
children.description: std::forward preserves the original value category of an argument when passing it on, so a factory like make_unique can construct objects without extra copies.

cpp.title: STL Containers and Algorithms
cpp.description: Use the C++ Standard Template Library containers (vector, map, set, unordered_map) and algorithms (sort, find, transform, erase_if) to write efficient, idiomatic C++, and handle dates and times with std::chrono. The STL is one of the most powerful standard libraries in any language.
cpp.challenge: Replace all raw arrays in the contact book with vector and unordered_map, and use STL algorithms for all searching and sorting operations.

children.title: Big-O for STL ops
children.description: std::vector provides O(1) random access and amortized O(1) push_back; std::map provides O(log n) ops; std::unordered_map provides O(1) average — choosing the right container matters.

children.title: Iterator categories
children.description: Iterators come in 6 categories (input, output, forward, bidirectional, random access, contiguous) — algorithms require specific categories, and using the wrong one causes compile errors.

children.title: Predicate-based algorithms
children.description: Most STL algorithms take a predicate (a function or lambda returning bool) to decide which elements to find, count or remove. To delete matching elements, call std::erase_if (C++20) instead of the old erase-remove idiom, which was easy to get wrong.

children.title: std::chrono dates and time zones
children.description: std::chrono gives type-safe durations and time points, so you cannot accidentally add seconds to milliseconds. Since C++20 it also covers calendar dates and IANA time zones, replacing hand-rolled date math and C functions like localtime.

children.title: vector vs deque vs list
children.description: vector is contiguous and cache-friendly for sequential access; deque supports efficient front/back insertion; list has O(1) splicing but poor cache performance.

children.title: unordered_map vs map
children.description: unordered_map provides O(1) average lookup using hashing; map provides O(log n) with sorted keys — use unordered_map unless you need ordering or a custom comparator.

children.title: std::sort and std::stable_sort
children.description: std::sort provides introsort (O(n log n) worst case); std::stable_sort preserves relative order of equal elements — prefer sort unless stability is required.

children.title: std::transform and std::for_each
children.description: transform applies a function to each element and writes results to another range; for_each applies a function for side effects — both replace explicit loops.

cpp.title: Templates and Generic Programming
cpp.description: Write function templates and class templates to create generic, reusable code that works across types without runtime overhead. C++ templates are Turing-complete and enable zero-cost abstractions unique to the language.

resources.label: C++ Templates: The Complete Guide (2nd ed.)

cpp.challenge: Add a generic Cache<K, V> template class to the contact book with configurable eviction policy, specializing it for string keys with case-insensitive lookup.

children.title: Compile-time code generation
children.description: Templates generate code at compile time for each type they're instantiated with — this is zero-runtime-overhead abstraction, but can increase binary size.

children.title: Template bloat
children.description: Instantiating the same template with many types creates many copies of the generated code — explicit instantiation declarations and the pimpl idiom mitigate this.

children.title: Full and partial specialization
children.description: Specialization lets you give a template a different implementation for specific types: full specialization for one exact type, partial specialization for a family such as all pointers. The standard library uses it, for example, to make std::vector<bool> pack bits.

children.title: Variadic templates
children.description: A parameter pack lets one template accept any number of arguments of any types, which is how std::make_unique, std::tuple and std::format are written. You expand the pack with ... and, since C++17, often process it in one line with a fold expression.

children.title: CRTP — Curiously Recurring Template Pattern
children.description: CRTP passes the derived class as a template argument to the base — enabling static polymorphism (no vtable) and mixin-style code reuse.

children.title: Policy-based design
children.description: Policy classes are template parameters that inject behaviour — separating concerns like allocation strategy from container logic for zero-cost customisation.

children.title: requires clauses
children.description: requires(T t) { t.size(); } specifies what operations a type must support — much clearer template errors than SFINAE, with better IDE support.

children.title: Standard concepts
children.description: The <concepts> header provides ready-made concepts (std::integral, std::floating_point, std::invocable) — use them instead of writing your own SFINAE checks.

cpp.title: Compile-Time C++: constexpr, Concepts, and Metaprogramming
cpp.description: Move work from run time to compile time and constrain templates with readable requirements. constexpr and consteval compute values during compilation, concepts replace SFINAE error walls with clear constraints, and fold expressions simplify variadic code.

resources.label: C++ Core Guidelines - Templates and generic programming

cpp.challenge: Build a compile-time lookup table and a fixed-size matrix type that are fully usable in constexpr contexts. Then write a constrained generic sum function using concepts, and use static_assert on your concept to check that unsuitable types are rejected.

children.title: constexpr functions
children.description: A constexpr function can run at compile time when its arguments are constants, and at run time otherwise. Since C++20 it may use dynamic allocation inside the evaluation, std::vector and std::string included.

children.title: consteval and constinit
children.description: consteval forces a function to be evaluated at compile time, and constinit guarantees a variable is initialized statically, which avoids the static initialization order problem.

children.title: Standard and custom concepts
children.description: A concept names a requirement on template arguments. The standard library provides ready-made ones such as std::integral, std::regular and std::ranges::range.

children.title: requires expressions
children.description: A requires expression checks that a set of expressions and types is valid, and returns a bool at compile time. It is how most custom concepts are written.

children.title: Type traits
children.description: The <type_traits> header lets templates ask questions about types, like whether one is trivially copyable, and select behavior at compile time. Prefer concepts over enable_if for new code.

children.title: Fold expressions and packs
children.description: A fold expression reduces a parameter pack with an operator in one line, replacing recursive variadic templates for sums, logical checks and printing.

children.title: static_assert and compile-time tests
children.description: static_assert turns a wrong assumption into a compile error with your own message. Combined with constexpr, it lets you test a function's results without running the program.

children.title: Replacing SFINAE with concepts
children.description: SFINAE hides overloads through substitution failures and produces unreadable errors. A concept constraint states the same rule directly and reports exactly which requirement failed.

cpp.title: Smart Pointers and Modern Memory Management
cpp.description: Replace raw pointers with smart pointers (unique_ptr, shared_ptr, weak_ptr) for automatic, safe memory management. Modern C++ code should rarely if ever use new and delete directly.
cpp.challenge: Refactor the entire contact book to use smart pointers exclusively, eliminating all raw new/delete, and demonstrate correct use of weak_ptr for observer relationships.

children.title: unique_ptr ownership model
children.description: unique_ptr represents exclusive ownership — it cannot be copied, only moved. When it goes out of scope, it automatically deletes the managed object.

children.title: shared_ptr reference counting
children.description: shared_ptr uses atomic reference counting — when the last copy is destroyed, the managed object is deleted. The shared control block has overhead; use unique_ptr when ownership is exclusive.

children.title: Breaking reference cycles
children.description: shared_ptr cycles prevent deletion — weak_ptr observes a shared_ptr without owning it, breaking the cycle and allowing proper cleanup.

children.title: lock() pattern
children.description: weak_ptr::lock() returns a shared_ptr if the managed object still exists, or an empty shared_ptr if it was already destroyed — always check before using.

children.title: make_unique and make_shared
children.description: Always use make_unique<T>(args) instead of new — it's exception-safe (no leak if constructor throws) and more readable. make_shared allocates the object and control block together.

children.title: Passing smart pointers
children.description: Pass by raw reference/pointer when ownership isn't transferred; pass unique_ptr by value to transfer ownership; pass shared_ptr by value to share ownership — passing by const& just to observe.

children.title: File handle RAII with unique_ptr
children.description: unique_ptr<FILE, decltype(&fclose)> wraps a C FILE* and calls fclose automatically — any custom cleanup can be injected as a deleter.

resources.label: C++ Core Guidelines - Smart pointer rules

children.title: Array deleters
children.description: unique_ptr<T[]> automatically uses delete[] instead of delete for array allocations — use it when you must manage raw arrays (rare with std::vector).

cpp.title: Lambdas, Ranges, and Modern C++ Idioms
cpp.description: Use C++11/14/17/20 modern idioms including lambdas, range-based for, structured bindings, and the Ranges library. Modern C++ reads very differently from legacy C++ - knowing the new idioms is essential.
cpp.challenge: Rewrite all contact book filtering and querying using C++20 Ranges with view pipelines, structured bindings for result unpacking, and std::optional for nullable results.

children.title: Closure object
children.description: A lambda creates an anonymous struct (closure type) with operator() — capturing variables copies or references them as data members of this struct.

children.title: Capture modes
children.description: [=] captures all locals by value; [&] by reference; [this] captures the this pointer — mixing them ([=, &x]) is allowed. Reference captures dangle if the lambda outlives the local.

children.title: Lazy evaluation
children.description: Range views are lazy — they don't compute anything until you iterate. Chaining views composes into a single pass over the data without intermediate containers.

children.title: std::optional and std::variant
children.description: std::optional<T> holds either a value or nothing, which is clearer than returning a null pointer or a magic -1. std::variant<A, B> holds exactly one of several types and, with std::visit, is a type-safe replacement for unions and many small class hierarchies.

children.title: Structured bindings (C++17)
children.description: auto [x, y] = pair; binds multiple variables from a struct, pair, or tuple in one line — cleaner than std::tie and works with custom types implementing get<>.

children.title: if constexpr
children.description: if constexpr(condition) evaluates the condition at compile time and discards the dead branch entirely — enabling template specialization logic without enable_if.

children.title: std::views::filter and transform
children.description: std::views::filter(pred) | std::views::transform(f) composes into a lazy pipeline — iterate once, no intermediate allocations, and composable with any range.

children.title: std::ranges algorithms
children.description: std::ranges::sort, std::ranges::find_if, and std::ranges::copy replace their iterator-pair counterparts — accepting containers directly and projections for member access.

cpp.title: Concurrency in C++
cpp.description: Write multi-threaded C++ programs using std::jthread, mutexes, condition variables, and atomics from the standard concurrency library. C++ concurrency requires explicit management - the memory model is the foundation.
cpp.challenge: Add a background auto-save std::jthread to the contact book that periodically serializes data and shuts down cleanly through its stop_token, using a mutex-protected queue for pending write operations.

children.title: Happens-before and memory orderings
children.description: C++'s memory model defines happens-before — std::memory_order controls how atomic operations synchronize between threads without locks.

children.title: Data races are UB
children.description: A data race (unsynchronized access where at least one is a write) is undefined behaviour in C++ — the compiler and CPU may reorder operations in ways that make the race worse.

children.title: Thread sanitizer (TSan)
children.description: Compile with -fsanitize=thread to detect data races at runtime — TSan instruments memory accesses and reports races with the exact thread and location.

children.title: std::atomic for lock-free programming
children.description: std::atomic<T> provides lock-free operations on simple types — use it instead of mutex for hot counters and flags where lock overhead matters.

children.title: std::jthread and stop_token
children.description: std::jthread (C++20) joins automatically in its destructor, so you cannot forget a join and crash the program the way you can with std::thread. It also carries a std::stop_token, a built-in way to ask the thread to finish its work and exit cleanly.

children.title: std::async and std::future
children.description: std::async launches a task asynchronously (or deferred) and returns a future — a higher-level alternative to raw threads for tasks that produce a result.

children.title: std::mutex and lock_guard
children.description: std::lock_guard<std::mutex> is an RAII wrapper that locks on construction and unlocks on destruction — the standard pattern for protecting shared state.

children.title: std::condition_variable
children.description: condition_variable allows one thread to wait until a condition is true — use with a unique_lock and a predicate to avoid spurious wakeups.

cpp.title: Coroutines and Modules (C++20/23)
cpp.description: Learn the two big C++20 language features that change how programs are structured. Coroutines let a function suspend and resume without blocking a thread, and modules replace textual header inclusion with compiled interfaces that build faster and leak fewer macros.
topics: Module interface units and import std

resources.label: Lewis Baker - C++ Coroutines: Understanding operator co_await

cpp.challenge: Write a coroutine that uses std::generator to stream the Fibonacci sequence and the lines of a file, then implement a minimal generator<T> by hand to see what the promise type does. Finally convert one library in your project from headers to a module built with CMake 3.28+ and compare build times before and after.

children.title: Promise type and handle
children.description: The compiler turns a coroutine into a state machine controlled by a promise type. A coroutine_handle lets you resume or destroy the suspended coroutine.

children.title: Suspension points
children.description: co_await decides at each point whether to suspend, through the awaiter's await_ready, await_suspend and await_resume functions.

children.title: std::generator (C++23)
children.description: std::generator is the standard coroutine type for lazy sequences: write a function that co_yields values and loop over it like a range. Before C++23 every project wrote its own generator class, so prefer the standard one where your compiler supports it.

children.title: Lifetime pitfalls
children.description: A coroutine's parameters are copied into its frame, but references still point at the caller's objects. If the caller returns first, the coroutine reads dangling memory.

children.title: Module interface units
children.description: A module interface unit declares what a module exports, and consumers write import instead of #include. Macros and private details no longer leak between files.

children.title: CMake 3.28+ and import std
children.description: Modules need the build system to scan sources and build interfaces in dependency order, which CMake supports natively from version 3.28 with FILE_SET CXX_MODULES. Newer toolchains also offer import std, which loads the whole standard library as one module instead of dozens of headers.

children.title: Migrating from headers
children.description: Convert leaf libraries first, keep the old headers during the transition, and measure build time before and after to see whether the change pays off for your project.

children.title: Header units and legacy code
children.description: A header unit lets you import an existing header as a module-like unit without rewriting it, as a bridge for code you cannot change yet.

cpp.title: Error Handling and Robust C++
cpp.description: Handle errors in C++ using exceptions, noexcept, std::error_code, and defensive programming techniques. C++ offers multiple error-handling strategies - choosing the right one for each context is a mark of expertise.
topics: RAII and copy-and-swap for exception safety

resources.label: isocpp FAQ - Exceptions and error handling

cpp.challenge: Add strong exception safety guarantees to all ContactBook mutating operations and use std::error_code for file I/O error reporting without throwing.

children.title: Basic, strong, nothrow guarantees
children.description: Exception safety levels: basic (invariants hold), strong (commit-or-rollback), nothrow (never throws). Most well-written C++ targets the strong guarantee for mutating operations.

children.title: RAII for exception safety
children.description: RAII objects clean up automatically when an exception unwinds the stack — this is what makes C++ exception handling practical without finally blocks.

children.title: Result type pattern
children.description: std::expected<T, E> either holds a value or an error — a zero-overhead alternative to exceptions for recoverable errors in performance-critical paths.

children.title: Error handling without exceptions
children.description: Embedded and real-time C++ often disables exceptions — std::expected, error_code, and output parameters are the alternatives with deterministic performance.

children.title: try/catch hierarchies
children.description: Catch exceptions from most specific to least specific — catching std::exception& first handles most standard library errors with a readable .what() message.

children.title: Custom exception classes
children.description: Derive from std::exception or std::runtime_error to create domain-specific exceptions — override what() to return a meaningful error description.

children.title: noexcept in move operations
children.description: Move constructors and move assignment operators should be noexcept — STL containers check this to decide whether to move or copy during reallocation.

children.title: Copy-and-swap idiom
children.description: Copy-and-swap implements assignment by copying the source into a temporary and then swapping it with *this using a noexcept swap. If the copy throws, the original object is untouched, so you get the strong exception guarantee almost for free.

resources.label: isocpp FAQ - Exceptions and error handling

cpp.title: Performance Engineering: Cache, Memory Layout, and Allocators
cpp.description: Learn why identical algorithms can differ by 10x in speed: cache behavior, data layout and allocation patterns usually matter more than instruction counts. Measure first with a benchmarking harness, then change layout and allocation strategy and verify the gain.
topics: CPU caches, cache lines and locality
Data layout: array of structs vs struct of arrays
Reading compiler output in Compiler Explorer
cpp.challenge: Take a particle simulation stored as an array of structs and benchmark it. Convert it to a struct of arrays, add a std::pmr monotonic arena for per-frame allocations, and report the measured speedup of each change separately.

children.title: Cache lines and locality
children.description: The CPU loads memory in cache lines, usually 64 bytes. Iterating contiguous data uses every byte loaded, while chasing pointers wastes most of each line.

children.title: False sharing and alignment
children.description: Two threads writing to different variables on the same cache line slow each other down. Align or pad hot data to separate lines.

children.title: AoS vs SoA
children.description: An array of structs keeps each object together; a struct of arrays keeps each field together. When a loop reads one field, SoA fits far more useful data per cache line.

children.title: Struct padding
children.description: The compiler inserts padding to align members, so reordering fields from largest to smallest can shrink a struct and fit more objects per cache line.

children.title: std::pmr and arena allocators
children.description: Polymorphic memory resources let containers draw from an arena you control. A monotonic arena makes per-frame or per-request allocation nearly free and frees everything at once.

children.title: Avoiding hidden allocations
children.description: Growing a vector, building strings and copying captured lambdas all allocate. Reserve capacity up front and watch for allocations inside hot loops.

children.title: Google Benchmark
children.description: A benchmark library handles warm-up, repetition and statistics so results are not noise. Always benchmark an optimized build and stop the compiler from deleting the work.

children.title: Reading compiler output
children.description: Compiler Explorer shows the assembly for your code at each optimization level, so you can check whether a loop was vectorized or a call was inlined.

cpp.title: Production C++ - Build Systems, Profiling, and Ecosystem
cpp.description: Build production C++ with CMake, test with GoogleTest or Catch2, debug with GDB and LLDB, profile with perf, catch bugs with sanitizers, and manage dependencies with vcpkg or Conan. Production C++ requires mastery of the full toolchain.
topics: CMake targets and modern CMake patterns
Unit testing with GoogleTest or Catch2
cpp.challenge: Finalize the contact book with a CMake build, a GoogleTest suite, an AddressSanitizer clean run, vcpkg- or Conan-managed dependencies, and a perf profile showing no hot spots in critical paths.

children.title: Modern CMake patterns
children.description: target_* commands (target_include_directories, target_link_libraries) with PRIVATE/PUBLIC/INTERFACE propagate dependencies correctly — never use global include_directories().

children.title: vcpkg and Conan
children.description: C++ has no single built-in package manager, so most teams pick vcpkg or Conan. vcpkg in manifest mode reads a vcpkg.json and plugs into CMake through a toolchain file; Conan 2 is more flexible for custom binary builds and private package servers.

children.title: gprof and perf
children.description: gprof instruments binaries at compile time; perf samples CPU counters with no recompilation — perf is more accurate for production code.

children.title: Compiler Sanitizers
children.description: -fsanitize=address,undefined,thread catches memory errors, UB, and data races respectively — run all three in your CI pipeline before shipping.

children.title: Unit testing with GoogleTest
children.description: GoogleTest is the most widely used C++ test framework: write TEST() cases with EXPECT_ and ASSERT_ checks and run them through CTest in CI. Catch2 is a popular lighter alternative with a more natural assertion syntax.

children.title: Debugging with GDB and LLDB
children.description: A debugger lets you stop a program at a breakpoint, step line by line, and inspect variables and the call stack, which finds crashes far faster than print statements. GDB is the standard on Linux with GCC, and LLDB is the LLVM debugger used with Clang and on macOS.

children.title: GitHub Actions for C++
children.description: A CMake + CTest workflow builds and tests in CI — add separate jobs for each sanitizer and for multiple compilers (GCC, Clang) to catch compiler-specific issues.

children.title: clang-tidy static analysis
children.description: clang-tidy provides hundreds of C++ lint checks — run it in CI with -warnings-as-errors to enforce coding style and catch common bugs before review.

csharp.title: C# Syntax and .NET Setup
csharp.description: Set up the .NET SDK, create and run C# projects with the dotnet CLI, and learn basic C# syntax. C# is a modern, statically typed language that runs on the .NET runtime across Windows, Linux, and macOS.
csharp.challenge: Build a command-line expense tracker in C# using the dotnet CLI, with add, list, and total commands.

children.title: CLR and managed execution
children.description: C# compiles to CIL (Common Intermediate Language) bytecode executed by the CLR — the runtime handles JIT compilation, garbage collection, and type safety across all .NET languages.

children.title: Value vs reference types
children.description: Value types (struct, int, bool) live on the stack and are copied on assignment; reference types (class, string, arrays) live on the heap with a pointer — understanding this drives boxing/unboxing awareness.

children.title: Unified type system
children.description: In C#, all types including primitives ultimately derive from System.Object — int is an alias for System.Int32, enabling methods like .ToString() on any value.

children.title: Nullable value types
children.description: int? is shorthand for Nullable<int> — a struct that wraps a value type to allow null. C# 8+ nullable reference types extend this safety to reference types.

children.title: .NET SDK and CLI
children.description: dotnet new, dotnet build, dotnet run, dotnet test — the .NET CLI handles everything from project scaffolding to publishing without an IDE.

children.title: Visual Studio vs VS Code
children.description: Visual Studio (Windows/Mac) provides the richest C# experience with full debugging and designer tools; VS Code + C# Dev Kit is cross-platform and lighter for modern .NET projects.

children.title: .csproj and solution files
children.description: .csproj is an MSBuild XML file defining targets, dependencies, and build options — .sln groups multiple projects together for building and IDE navigation.

children.title: NuGet package management
children.description: NuGet is the .NET package manager — add packages with dotnet add package or the NuGet Package Manager in Visual Studio. packages.lock.json pins exact versions for reproducible builds.

csharp.title: Object-Oriented C#
csharp.description: Use C# classes, inheritance, interfaces, and properties to build structured object-oriented programs. C# OOP has several features not found in Java - properties, partial classes, and explicit interface implementation among them.
csharp.challenge: Refactor the expense tracker into an OOP design with Expense, Category, and Budget classes using properties and interface-based storage.

children.title: Class vs struct semantics
children.description: Classes are reference types with heap allocation and inheritance; structs are value types with stack allocation and copy semantics — structs are ideal for small, immutable data like coordinates.

children.title: Virtual, override, and sealed
children.description: virtual declares a method overridable; override replaces it in a subclass; sealed prevents further overriding or class inheritance — together they control the extensibility contract.

children.title: Explicit interface implementation
children.description: When a class implements two interfaces with the same method name, explicit implementation disambiguates — the method is only accessible through the interface type, not the class type.

children.title: Default interface methods (C# 8+)
children.description: Interfaces can now have default method implementations — enabling interface evolution without breaking existing implementations, similar to Java 8 default methods.

children.title: Properties vs fields
children.description: Properties encapsulate fields with get/set accessors — auto-properties ({ get; set; }) generate a backing field automatically, while computed properties derive from other state.

children.title: Init-only properties and records
children.description: init accessors (C# 9+) allow setting a property only during object initialization — records combine init properties, value equality, and with-expressions for immutable data models.

children.title: Constructor injection pattern
children.description: Declaring dependencies as constructor parameters makes them explicit and testable — the .NET built-in DI container (IServiceCollection) resolves them automatically.

children.title: Service lifetimes
children.description: Transient (new instance per request), Scoped (per HTTP request), and Singleton (one instance per app) — choosing the wrong lifetime causes subtle bugs like disposed DbContext.

csharp.title: Collections, Generics, and LINQ Basics
csharp.description: Use .NET generic collections (List<T>, Dictionary<K,V>, HashSet<T>) and write your first LINQ queries to filter and project data. LINQ is one of C# most distinctive and powerful features.
csharp.challenge: Use LINQ to add reporting features to the expense tracker - top categories, monthly totals, and expenses above a threshold - using method chaining.

children.title: Deferred vs immediate execution
children.description: LINQ query operators like Where and Select are lazy — they return IEnumerable<T> without executing until iterated. ToList(), Count(), and First() trigger immediate execution.

children.title: Expression trees
children.description: LINQ to SQL and Entity Framework translate LINQ queries to SQL by building expression trees — an in-memory representation of code as data that can be analyzed and transformed.

children.title: Reified generics vs type erasure
children.description: Unlike Java, .NET generics are reified — List<int> and List<string> are genuinely different types at runtime. This enables runtime typeof(T) checks and avoids boxing for value types.

children.title: Covariance and contravariance
children.description: out T makes a generic type covariant (IEnumerable<string> assignable to IEnumerable<object>); in T makes it contravariant — only applicable to interfaces and delegates.

children.title: Method syntax vs query syntax
children.description: LINQ has two syntaxes — method chaining (.Where().Select()) and SQL-like query expressions (from x in xs where ... select). Method syntax is more common and composable.

children.title: GroupBy, Join, and SelectMany
children.description: GroupBy groups elements by a key; Join correlates two sequences; SelectMany flattens nested collections — the three LINQ operators that handle relational-style data transformation.

children.title: IEnumerable<T> vs IQueryable<T>
children.description: IEnumerable<T> executes LINQ in memory; IQueryable<T> translates LINQ to a query language (SQL) — mixing them accidentally causes the N+1 query problem in Entity Framework.

children.title: List<T>, Dictionary<K,V>, HashSet<T>
children.description: List<T> for ordered sequences, Dictionary<K,V> for key-value lookups, HashSet<T> for unique elements — all implement generic interfaces enabling LINQ and polymorphic code.

csharp.title: Exception Handling and File I/O
csharp.description: Write robust exception handling using C# try/catch/finally, custom exceptions, and the using statement for resource management. Use System.IO for file operations and System.Text.Json for serialization.
csharp.challenge: Add JSON file persistence to the expense tracker using System.Text.Json with custom exceptions for invalid data and a using statement for file handle safety.

children.title: Exception hierarchy
children.description: All C# exceptions derive from System.Exception — System.ApplicationException (app errors) and System.SystemException (runtime errors) are the two main branches, though the distinction is rarely enforced.

children.title: Exception filters
children.description: catch (IOException e) when (e.HResult == -2147024784) — catch filters conditionally handle exceptions without catching and rethrowing, which preserves the original stack trace.

children.title: Stream hierarchy
children.description: Stream is the abstract base for all I/O in .NET — FileStream, MemoryStream, NetworkStream all share the same Read/Write interface enabling composable stream pipelines.

children.title: IDisposable and using
children.description: Resources implementing IDisposable must be disposed — the using statement calls Dispose() automatically on scope exit, even on exceptions. C# 8+ using declarations remove the nesting.

children.title: Custom exceptions
children.description: Derive from Exception (or a specific subtype) and add properties for domain context — throw new OrderNotFoundException(orderId) is more informative than throw new Exception("not found").

children.title: Global exception handling
children.description: ASP.NET Core's UseExceptionHandler middleware catches unhandled exceptions globally — the right place to map exceptions to HTTP status codes and log them centrally.

children.title: File and Directory classes
children.description: System.IO.File provides static methods for common operations (File.ReadAllText, File.WriteAllLines, File.Exists) — the quickest path for simple file tasks without stream management.

children.title: StreamReader and StreamWriter
children.description: StreamReader/Writer wrap streams with text encoding support — use them with using for reading/writing text files line by line without loading everything into memory.

csharp.title: Async/Await and the Task Parallel Library
csharp.description: Write asynchronous C# code using async/await and the Task Parallel Library for non-blocking I/O and parallel CPU work. C# async/await is one of the most ergonomic async models in any mainstream language.
csharp.challenge: Add async file I/O and an async HTTP export feature to the expense tracker using async/await throughout with CancellationToken support.

children.title: State machine compilation
children.description: The C# compiler transforms async methods into state machines — each await point is a state, and the runtime schedules continuation without blocking a thread.

children.title: SynchronizationContext
children.description: SynchronizationContext captures the current thread context — in UI apps, await resumes on the UI thread by default. ConfigureAwait(false) avoids this capture for library code.

children.title: Task vs Thread
children.description: Task represents a unit of work scheduled on the ThreadPool — more efficient than raw Thread for short operations, and composable with async/await unlike Thread.

children.title: CancellationToken
children.description: CancellationToken is the standard way to cancel async operations in .NET — pass it through the call chain and check IsCancellationRequested or use ThrowIfCancellationRequested.

children.title: async void — avoid it
children.description: async void methods can't be awaited and swallow exceptions silently — only use it for event handlers. Prefer async Task for everything else.

children.title: Task.WhenAll and Task.WhenAny
children.description: Task.WhenAll runs multiple async operations in parallel and waits for all; Task.WhenAny completes when the first finishes — the async equivalents of Promise.all and Promise.race.

children.title: IHttpClientFactory
children.description: Register IHttpClientFactory in DI instead of newing HttpClient — it manages connection pooling and lifetime, preventing socket exhaustion from too many short-lived HttpClient instances.

children.title: Typed HTTP clients
children.description: A typed client wraps IHttpClientFactory with a strongly typed API for a specific backend — encapsulating base URL, auth headers, and retry policies in one place.

csharp.title: Advanced LINQ and Functional Patterns
csharp.description: Go deeper with LINQ including grouping, joining, and custom operators, and apply functional patterns like immutable records and expression trees. LINQ's composability enables a functional style that integrates naturally with C# OOP.
csharp.challenge: Replace all expense filtering with advanced LINQ pipelines using GroupBy for category reports, switch expressions for expense classification, and immutable record types.

children.title: Custom LINQ operators
children.description: Extension methods on IEnumerable<T> create reusable LINQ operators — yield return enables lazy, composable sequences without loading all data into memory.

children.title: Queryable vs Enumerable
children.description: Enumerable extension methods operate in memory; Queryable methods build expression trees translated to SQL by ORMs — accidentally calling AsEnumerable() too early loads all rows into memory.

children.title: Immutability with records and init
children.description: record and init-only properties enable immutable data models with value semantics — the with expression creates a modified copy without mutating the original.

children.title: Pattern matching switch expressions
children.description: C# 8+ switch expressions with type patterns and when guards enable concise, exhaustive transformation logic without if/else chains.

children.title: Avoiding N+1 queries
children.description: Using Include() for eager loading and selecting only needed columns with Select() prevents the N+1 query problem and large data over-fetching in Entity Framework.

children.title: AsNoTracking for read-only queries
children.description: AsNoTracking() skips change tracking for read-only queries — significantly faster for queries where you don't need to save changes back to the database.

children.title: LanguageExt
children.description: LanguageExt brings Haskell-inspired types (Option, Either, Try) to C# — enabling railway-oriented programming and eliminating null reference exceptions structurally.

children.title: Memoization and lazy evaluation
children.description: Lazy<T> defers expensive initialization until first access and caches the result — the built-in .NET solution for lazy singletons and expensive computations.

csharp.title: Dependency Injection and Architecture Patterns
csharp.description: Understand dependency injection as built into .NET, and apply common architecture patterns (repository, service layer, options pattern) used throughout the .NET ecosystem. DI is not a framework choice in .NET - it is a core platform feature.
csharp.challenge: Refactor the expense tracker to use the .NET DI container with constructor-injected services, a repository interface, and ILogger for structured logging.

children.title: IServiceCollection and IServiceProvider
children.description: IServiceCollection is the registration container; IServiceProvider resolves instances — the entire .NET ecosystem (ASP.NET Core, EF Core, logging) is built around this abstraction.

children.title: Decorator pattern with DI
children.description: Registering a service multiple times lets you wrap implementations with decorators — Scrutor library adds TryDecorate<IService, Decorator>() for cleaner registration.

children.title: Onion / Hexagonal architecture
children.description: Domain logic at the center, infrastructure at the edges — dependencies point inward, making the domain layer framework-agnostic and easily testable.

children.title: CQRS pattern
children.description: Command Query Responsibility Segregation separates read and write models — MediatR is the standard .NET library for dispatching commands and queries without direct service references.

children.title: Repository pattern
children.description: Repository wraps data access behind an interface — swapping EF Core for Dapper or an in-memory store for testing requires only a new implementation, not changing business logic.

children.title: Unit of Work
children.description: Unit of Work groups multiple repository operations into a single transaction — EF Core's DbContext already implements this pattern; explicit UoW is only needed for complex multi-context scenarios.

resources.label: Unit of Work Pattern in C#

children.title: ASP.NET Core middleware pipeline
children.description: Middleware components form an ordered pipeline — each calls next() to pass to the next component. Order matters: authentication before authorization, logging before everything.

children.title: MediatR pipeline behaviors
children.description: IPipelineBehavior<TRequest, TResponse> wraps every MediatR request — use it for cross-cutting concerns like validation, logging, and caching without modifying handlers.

csharp.title: Testing with xUnit and Moq
csharp.description: Write unit and integration tests using xUnit, mock dependencies with Moq, and measure coverage. The .NET testing ecosystem is mature and well-integrated with the dotnet CLI and CI systems.
csharp.challenge: Write an xUnit test suite for the expense tracker using Moq for storage dependencies, Theory tests for edge cases, and FluentAssertions for readable assertions.

children.title: xUnit design philosophy
children.description: xUnit was designed with testability in mind — no [SetUp]/[TearDown], just constructor/IDisposable. Each test gets a fresh instance, preventing shared state bugs.

children.title: Test isolation
children.description: Tests should be isolated — no shared state between test methods. Use fresh instances, in-memory databases, and mock dependencies to ensure tests are deterministic.

resources.label: Unit Testing Best Practices in C#

children.title: Castle DynamicProxy
children.description: Moq uses Castle DynamicProxy to generate mock implementations at runtime — this is why you can only mock virtual methods and interfaces; sealed/non-virtual methods can't be intercepted.

children.title: Setup and Verify
children.description: Setup() configures mock return values and behaviors; Verify() asserts that a method was called with specific arguments — both use lambda expressions for type-safe configuration.

children.title: FluentAssertions
children.description: FluentAssertions replaces Assert.Equal with result.Should().Be(expected) — producing human-readable failure messages with rich diff output for collections and objects.

children.title: AutoFixture for test data
children.description: AutoFixture generates anonymous test data automatically — eliminating manual test object construction and keeping tests focused on the behavior being tested.

children.title: WebApplicationFactory
children.description: WebApplicationFactory<Program> creates an in-memory test server for ASP.NET Core — enables full integration tests against real HTTP endpoints without a running server.

children.title: Respawn for database cleanup
children.description: Respawn resets a test database to a clean state between tests by intelligently deleting rows in dependency order — faster than recreating the schema for each test.

csharp.title: Modern C# Features - Nullable Reference Types, Spans, and Channels
csharp.description: Enable nullable reference types to eliminate null reference exceptions at compile time, use Span<T> for allocation-free data processing, and use System.Threading.Channels for async producer-consumer patterns. These features characterize modern, performance-conscious C#.
csharp.challenge: Enable nullable reference types across the expense tracker with zero warnings, add an IAsyncEnumerable export stream, and use Channels for a background notification pipeline.

children.title: Nullable reference types (C# 8+)
children.description: Enabling <Nullable>enable</Nullable> makes the compiler track null flow — string is non-nullable by default, string? is nullable, eliminating most NullReferenceExceptions at compile time.

children.title: Span<T> and Memory<T>
children.description: Span<T> is a stack-only slice over any contiguous memory (arrays, stack, unmanaged) — enables zero-copy string parsing and buffer manipulation without heap allocation.

children.title: System.Threading.Channels
children.description: Channel<T> provides a bounded or unbounded async-friendly producer-consumer queue — the modern replacement for BlockingCollection<T> in async pipelines.

children.title: IAsyncEnumerable<T>
children.description: async foreach iterates over an IAsyncEnumerable<T> — the async-native way to stream results from a database or API without buffering the entire result set.

children.title: ArrayPool<T>
children.description: ArrayPool<T>.Shared.Rent(size) returns a pooled array and Shared.Return() gives it back — eliminating GC pressure for hot paths that repeatedly allocate temporary arrays.

children.title: ref struct and stack allocation
children.description: ref struct types (like Span<T>) can only live on the stack — preventing heap allocation and GC interaction entirely for temporary high-performance operations.

children.title: Compile-time code generation
children.description: Source generators add code to a compilation at compile time — used by System.Text.Json, regex, and logging for zero-overhead serialization and pattern matching.

children.title: Incremental generators
children.description: Incremental source generators only re-run when their inputs change — critical for IDE performance, as classic generators re-ran on every keystroke.

csharp.title: Production C# - NuGet, Performance, and Ecosystem
csharp.description: Publish NuGet packages, profile .NET apps with dotnet-trace and BenchmarkDotNet, and survey the .NET ecosystem for web, desktop, and cloud development. Production .NET requires understanding the full platform beyond the language itself.
topics: Ecosystem overview (ASP.NET Core, EF Core, MAUI, Blazor)
csharp.challenge: Package the expense tracker core library as a NuGet package, run BenchmarkDotNet benchmarks on LINQ queries, publish results, and add a GitHub Actions workflow with test and publish steps.

children.title: Publishing modes
children.description: dotnet publish -c Release --self-contained true --runtime linux-x64 creates a self-contained executable; -p:PublishSingleFile=true bundles everything into one binary.

children.title: Native AOT compilation
children.description: .NET 7+ Native AOT compiles directly to native code at build time — instant startup, minimal memory, and no JIT overhead. Required for some performance-critical and embedded scenarios.

children.title: dotnet-trace and dotnet-counters
children.description: dotnet-trace collects CPU and allocation profiles; dotnet-counters monitors live metrics — both work on running processes without restarting or modifying the application.

children.title: BenchmarkDotNet
children.description: BenchmarkDotNet is the standard .NET micro-benchmarking library — it handles warm-up, statistical analysis, and hardware counter measurements for reliable performance comparisons.

children.title: ASP.NET Core
children.description: ASP.NET Core is the cross-platform web framework — minimal APIs for microservices, MVC for full-stack apps, SignalR for real-time, and gRPC for high-performance RPC.

children.title: Entity Framework Core
children.description: EF Core is the ORM for .NET — code-first migrations, LINQ queries translated to SQL, and support for SQL Server, PostgreSQL, SQLite, and MySQL.

children.title: GitHub Actions for .NET
children.description: actions/setup-dotnet installs the SDK; dotnet restore, build, test, and publish form the standard CI pipeline with NuGet caching for fast builds.

children.title: Docker for .NET apps
children.description: Multi-stage builds with the official mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk builder and mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet runtime image produce lean production containers.

ruby.title: Ruby Syntax and the Ruby Way
ruby.description: Install Ruby with rbenv or rvm, learn the fundamental syntax, and begin developing a feel for Ruby's philosophy of developer happiness and expressiveness. Ruby is designed to be read like natural language - idiomatic Ruby embraces this.
ruby.challenge: Build a command-line quiz game in Ruby that reads questions from a YAML file, tracks score, and runs in a tight game loop.

children.title: Principle of Least Surprise
children.description: Ruby is designed to minimize surprise for experienced programmers — Matz optimized for developer happiness, meaning code reads like natural language and behaves predictably.

children.title: Everything is an object
children.description: In Ruby, every value including integers, booleans, and nil is an object with methods — 1.class returns Integer, nil.nil? returns true, true.&(false) works fine.

resources.label: Everything is an Object in Ruby

children.title: Duck typing
children.description: Ruby checks if an object responds to a method, not what class it belongs to — respond_to?(:each) is the Ruby way to test capability rather than inheritance.

children.title: Open classes
children.description: Any class in Ruby can be reopened and modified at runtime — adding methods to String or Integer is valid and widely used (though dangerous if overused).

children.title: rbenv and version management
children.description: rbenv manages multiple Ruby versions per project via .ruby-version — use it alongside bundler so every project has isolated, reproducible gem dependencies.

children.title: IRB and Pry
children.description: IRB is Ruby's built-in REPL; Pry adds syntax highlighting, navigation, and debugging capabilities — binding.pry drops into a REPL at any point in your code.

children.title: RuboCop for linting
children.description: RuboCop enforces the community Ruby style guide with auto-correct — configure it with .rubocop.yml to adopt the standard gradually without rewriting everything at once.

children.title: Idiomatic Ruby patterns
children.description: Prefer unless over if !condition, use symbol-to-proc (&:method), favour map/select/reduce over loops — these patterns signal Ruby fluency.

ruby.title: Collections - Arrays, Hashes, and Enumerables
ruby.description: Master Ruby arrays, hashes, and the Enumerable module which provides an incredibly rich set of collection methods. Enumerable is one of the most elegant parts of the Ruby language and is used throughout idiomatic Ruby code.
ruby.challenge: Add leaderboard tracking to the quiz game using hashes, sort and filter results with Enumerable methods, and export scores to a CSV using map.

children.title: Enumerable module
children.description: Including Enumerable in any class that implements each gives it 50+ methods (map, select, sort, group_by, etc.) — this is how Ruby's mixin system provides behaviour composition.

children.title: Lazy enumerators
children.description: array.lazy.map { }.select { }.first(5) evaluates only enough elements to satisfy the request — essential for working with infinite sequences or large data sets.

children.title: Symbol vs string keys
children.description: Symbols are immutable and interned — the same symbol object is reused everywhere, making them more memory-efficient than strings as hash keys.

children.title: Hash as keyword arguments
children.description: Ruby 2.0+ uses hashes as keyword arguments; Ruby 3.0 made the separation strict — understanding the distinction prevents ArgumentError in modern Ruby.

children.title: map, select, reduce, flat_map
children.description: These four methods cover most data transformation needs — map transforms, select filters, reduce aggregates, flat_map transforms and flattens in one pass.

children.title: group_by and tally
children.description: group_by partitions a collection by a computed key; tally (Ruby 2.7+) counts occurrences — both replace common manual reduce patterns.

children.title: Range objects
children.description: (1..10) creates an inclusive range; (1...10) excludes the end — ranges work with integers, strings, and any Comparable object, and include the Enumerable module.

children.title: Endless and beginless ranges
children.description: (1..) and (..10) are Ruby 2.6+ endless/beginless ranges — used in case expressions and array slicing without needing Float::INFINITY.

ruby.title: Blocks, Procs, and Lambdas
ruby.description: Understand Ruby blocks as first-class constructs, the difference between Proc and Lambda, and how to write methods that yield to blocks. Blocks are the foundation of Ruby's DSL capabilities and iterative APIs.
ruby.challenge: Refactor the quiz game to use blocks for question rendering, add a timing feature using yield with a timer block, and create a configurable scoring lambda.

children.title: yield and block_given?
children.description: yield passes control to the caller's block; block_given? checks if one was provided — the foundation of Ruby's iterator and DSL patterns.

children.title: Explicit block capture with &
children.description: def method(&block) captures the block as a Proc object — store it, pass it to other methods, or call it later with block.call or block.().

children.title: Return behavior difference
children.description: return inside a Proc returns from the enclosing method; return inside a Lambda returns from the lambda only — this makes lambdas safer for use as callbacks.

children.title: Arity checking
children.description: Lambdas enforce the correct number of arguments (like methods); Procs silently accept wrong arity — use lambdas when argument count correctness matters.

children.title: Symbol to proc (&:method)
children.description: [1,2,3].map(&:to_s) converts the :to_s symbol to a Proc calling to_s on each element — a concise shorthand for single-method lambdas.

children.title: Enumerator and external iteration
children.description: enum = [1,2,3].each creates an Enumerator — call enum.next manually for external iteration, or pass it to methods expecting a block.

children.title: Method objects
children.description: method(:puts) returns a Method object that wraps a method as a callable — enables passing methods where blocks are expected without a wrapper lambda.

children.title: Curry for partial application
children.description: add = ->(a,b){ a+b }; add5 = add.curry.(5) — curry returns a new lambda with some arguments pre-filled, enabling partial application.

ruby.title: Object-Oriented Ruby
ruby.description: Build Ruby classes with the initialize method, attr_accessor, modules for mixins, and understand Ruby's open class model. Ruby OOP is dynamic and flexible - classes can be reopened and modified at any time.
ruby.challenge: Refactor the quiz game into a full OOP design with Quiz, Question, Player, and Leaderboard classes, using the Comparable mixin for player ranking.

children.title: Method lookup path
children.description: Ruby searches the object's singleton class, then its class, then each included module (in reverse inclusion order), then the superclass chain — understanding this prevents method resolution surprises.

children.title: Singleton classes
children.description: Every Ruby object has a singleton class (eigenclass) that holds object-specific methods — class methods on a class are instance methods of that class's singleton class.

children.title: include vs extend vs prepend
children.description: include adds module methods as instance methods; extend adds them as class methods on the receiver; prepend inserts the module before the class in the lookup path for method wrapping.

children.title: Comparable and Enumerable modules
children.description: Including Comparable and implementing <=> gives you <, >, <=, >=, between?, and clamp for free. Including Enumerable and implementing each gives 50+ collection methods.

children.title: attr_accessor, attr_reader, attr_writer
children.description: These macros generate getter/setter methods — attr_accessor :name defines both name and name=, eliminating boilerplate instance variable accessors.

children.title: Struct for data classes
children.description: Struct.new(:name, :age) creates a class with accessors, ==, to_s, and to_a for free — lighter than a full class for simple value objects.

children.title: super keyword
children.description: super calls the same-named method in the parent class — super with no args passes the current method's args, super() passes none, super(args) passes explicit args.

children.title: method_missing and respond_to_missing?
children.description: method_missing intercepts calls to undefined methods — powerful for DSLs and proxies, but always implement respond_to_missing? alongside it for correct respond_to? behavior.

ruby.title: Metaprogramming Fundamentals
ruby.description: Begin exploring Ruby's metaprogramming capabilities - method_missing, define_method, send, and class macros - which enable Ruby's expressive DSLs and frameworks. Metaprogramming is where Ruby becomes truly unique.
ruby.challenge: Add a DSL to the quiz game that allows defining questions declaratively using class macros (e.g., question 'What is...?' do ... end) powered by define_method.

children.title: define_method and class_eval
children.description: define_method(:name) { body } creates a method dynamically at runtime; class_eval evaluates a string or block in the context of the class — the building blocks of all Ruby DSLs.

children.title: send and public_send
children.description: send(:method_name, args) calls any method including private ones; public_send respects visibility — both enable dynamic dispatch when the method name is only known at runtime.

children.title: included, extended, prepended hooks
children.description: These hooks fire when a module is mixed in — used by frameworks (ActiveSupport, Devise) to set up class-level configuration when a module is included.

children.title: inherited and method_added hooks
children.description: inherited(subclass) fires when a class is subclassed; method_added(name) fires when a method is defined — both enable framework-level introspection and automation.

children.title: instance_eval for DSLs
children.description: instance_eval executes a block in the context of an object — enabling the clean { } DSL syntax used by frameworks like RSpec and Rake.

children.title: Proc and block-based configuration
children.description: Accepting a block for configuration (MyClass.new { |c| c.option = value }) is idiomatic Ruby for optional setup — popular in test frameworks and gem configuration.

children.title: instance_variables and methods
children.description: instance_variables returns all @ variables; methods returns all available methods; instance_method(:name) retrieves an unbound method object for inspection.
