children.title: ObjectSpace for runtime introspection
children.description: ObjectSpace.each_object(ClassName) iterates over all live instances of a class — used by test frameworks and memory profilers to inspect the object graph.

ruby.title: Exception Handling and File I/O
ruby.description: Handle exceptions idiomatically in Ruby using rescue, ensure, retry, and custom exception classes, and read and write files and JSON. Ruby exception handling is concise - many operations have built-in rescue shorthand.
ruby.challenge: Add JSON persistence to the quiz game leaderboard with custom exceptions for file corruption, retry logic for transient I/O errors, and ensure for cleanup.

children.title: Exception vs StandardError
children.description: rescue with no class catches StandardError and below — never rescue Exception as it catches SignalException and SystemExit, preventing clean shutdown.

children.title: ensure and else clauses
children.description: ensure runs whether or not an exception was raised (like finally); else runs only when no exception was raised — both complement rescue in begin/end blocks.

children.title: IO and File hierarchy
children.description: File inherits from IO — all IO methods (read, write, gets, puts, seek) are available on File objects. File.open with a block auto-closes the file via ensure.

children.title: StringIO for in-memory streams
children.description: StringIO acts as a File-compatible IO object backed by a String — useful for testing code that writes to IO without creating actual files.

children.title: retry in rescue blocks
children.description: retry re-executes the begin block after a rescue — use with a counter to limit retries for transient errors like network timeouts.

children.title: raise with custom exceptions
children.description: Create domain exceptions with class OrderNotFoundError < StandardError; end — rescue OrderNotFoundError is more precise than rescuing all StandardErrors.

children.title: File.read, write, and foreach
children.description: File.read(path) returns the whole file as a string; File.foreach(path) iterates line by line without loading everything into memory — choose based on file size.

children.title: Pathname for path manipulation
children.description: Pathname wraps path strings with a rich API (/, +, glob, children, exist?) — cleaner than string concatenation for file path manipulation.

ruby.title: Gems and Bundler
ruby.description: Create and publish Ruby gems, manage dependencies with Bundler and Gemfile, and understand gem versioning. The Ruby gem ecosystem is vast - learning to navigate it and create gems yourself is essential.
topics: gem dependencies and runtime vs development
ruby.challenge: Package the quiz game as a gem with a Gemfile, gemspec, and a command-line binary, and publish it to a local gem server.

children.title: Gem structure and gemspec
children.description: A gem is a packaged Ruby library with a .gemspec defining its name, version, dependencies, and files — understanding the structure is essential for creating and maintaining gems.

children.title: Load path and require
children.description: require adds a file to the load path and executes it once; require_relative loads relative to the current file — Bundler manages the load path so gem requires work in any environment.

children.title: Gemfile and Gemfile.lock
children.description: Gemfile declares gem dependencies with version constraints; Gemfile.lock pins exact resolved versions — commit Gemfile.lock for applications, but not for libraries.

children.title: bundle exec
children.description: bundle exec runs a command in the context of the current bundle — ensures the correct gem versions are loaded rather than whatever is installed globally.

children.title: Faraday and HTTParty for HTTP
children.description: Faraday is a composable HTTP client with middleware support; HTTParty is simpler for straightforward API clients — both are widely used alternatives to net/http.

children.title: Dry-rb ecosystem
children.description: dry-validation, dry-types, and dry-monads bring functional programming concepts to Ruby — popular for building robust, well-typed service objects in non-Rails contexts.

children.title: Semantic versioning for gems
children.description: Follow semver strictly — patch for bug fixes, minor for new features, major for breaking changes. Users rely on ~> constraints which only allow patch/minor updates.

children.title: rake release and gem push
children.description: rake release tags the version in git and pushes to rubygems.org; configure trusted publishing with GitHub Actions for automated, secure releases.

ruby.title: Testing with RSpec
ruby.description: Write expressive, behavior-driven tests using RSpec with describe, context, and it blocks, and mock with RSpec mocks or Mocha. RSpec's DSL makes tests read almost like documentation.
ruby.challenge: Write a complete RSpec suite for the quiz game covering all classes, using doubles for file I/O, shared examples for game rules, and SimpleCov for coverage reporting.

children.title: describe, context, and it blocks
children.description: describe groups tests by subject; context groups by scenario; it describes expected behavior — three levels of nesting produce readable, hierarchical test output.

children.title: Subject and let memoization
children.description: let(:name) { expr } creates a memoized lazy helper — evaluated once per example and reset between examples. let! forces eager evaluation; subject is the implicit test target.

children.title: Mocks vs stubs vs spies
children.description: double creates a strict mock that only responds to configured messages; allow sets up stubs; expect sets up message expectations — RSpec's terminology matches Fowler's definitions.

children.title: instance_double and verified doubles
children.description: instance_double(:ClassName) verifies that stubbed methods actually exist on the class — prevents tests from silently passing after a method rename.

children.title: Shared examples
children.description: shared_examples_for 'a collection' { } defines reusable test groups — include them with it_behaves_like to verify that multiple classes fulfill the same contract.

children.title: FactoryBot for test data
children.description: FactoryBot defines factory templates for ActiveRecord models — create(:user, role: :admin) produces a valid instance without specifying every attribute.

children.title: DatabaseCleaner for test isolation
children.description: DatabaseCleaner resets the database between tests using truncation or transaction strategies — essential for keeping integration tests independent and repeatable.

children.title: VCR for HTTP interactions
children.description: VCR records real HTTP interactions to cassette files and replays them in tests — eliminating flaky tests that depend on external APIs being available.

ruby.title: Advanced Metaprogramming and DSL Design
ruby.description: Build internal DSLs using instance_eval, class_eval, and the full suite of Ruby metaprogramming tools. Understanding how Rails, RSpec, and Sinatra build their DSLs will make you a far more capable Ruby developer.
ruby.challenge: Build a configuration DSL for the quiz game using instance_eval so game settings can be expressed as a clean Ruby block without hash syntax.

children.title: BasicObject and blank slate
children.description: BasicObject has almost no methods — subclassing it creates a 'blank slate' object ideal for proxies and DSLs where inherited methods like class or inspect would interfere.

children.title: Kernel methods and mixins
children.description: Kernel is mixed into Object — methods like puts, p, require, and lambda are actually Kernel instance methods available everywhere, not top-level functions.

children.title: Fluent interfaces with method chaining
children.description: Returning self from methods enables chaining — query.where(active: true).order(:name).limit(10). This pattern is used by ActiveRecord, Arel, and most Ruby query builders.

children.title: Refinements for scoped monkey patching
children.description: Refinements activate monkey patches only within a specific scope (using MyRefinement) — safer than global open classes for adding methods to core types.

children.title: Frozen string literals
children.description: # frozen_string_literal: true at the top of a file makes all string literals immutable — reducing object allocations significantly in hot paths.

children.title: StackProf for CPU profiling
children.description: StackProf is a sampling profiler for Ruby — run your code with StackProf.run { } and call .report to see which methods consume the most CPU time.

children.title: Rails vs Sinatra vs Hanami
children.description: Rails is full-stack and convention-heavy; Sinatra is minimal for small APIs; Hanami is a clean-architecture alternative — choose based on project scale and team conventions.

children.title: Concurrent-ruby for threading
children.description: concurrent-ruby provides thread-safe data structures (Concurrent::Array, Concurrent::Hash) and higher-level concurrency primitives (Future, Promise) for production Ruby apps.

ruby.title: Production Ruby - Concurrency, Performance, and Ecosystem
ruby.description: Understand Ruby's GIL and concurrency options (threads, Ractors, async gem), profile Ruby code with ruby-prof and stackprof, and survey the production Ruby ecosystem. Ruby's production maturity is demonstrated by decades of Rails applications running at scale.
ruby.challenge: Add concurrent question fetching to the quiz game using Ruby threads with Mutex protection, profile the hot path with stackprof, and document an upgrade path to Ractors.

children.title: GIL and thread limitations
children.description: MRI Ruby has a Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) that prevents true parallel thread execution — threads are useful for I/O-bound work but not CPU-bound parallelism. Use Ractors or JRuby for CPU parallelism.

children.title: Ractors for true parallelism
children.description: Ractors (Ruby 3.0+) are actor-model concurrency units that run in parallel without the GIL — each Ractor has isolated state, communicating only via message passing.

children.title: MJIT and YJIT compilers
children.description: YJIT (Ruby 3.1+, written in Rust) is a lazy basic block versioning JIT compiler — delivers 20-40% speedups on real Rails applications with no code changes required.

children.title: memory_profiler and derailed_benchmarks
children.description: memory_profiler tracks per-line allocations; derailed_benchmarks measures memory usage of Rails apps at startup and per request — the standard toolkit for Ruby memory optimization.

children.title: Sidekiq for background jobs
children.description: Sidekiq processes background jobs using Redis and threads — the standard Ruby background job library with a web UI, retries, and scheduling built in.

children.title: Puma for web serving
children.description: Puma is the default Rails web server — multi-threaded, handles concurrent requests efficiently, and supports clustered mode for multi-process deployment.

children.title: GitHub Actions for Ruby
children.description: actions/setup-ruby with a .ruby-version file and bundle cache gives you a fast, reproducible CI pipeline — add rubocop and rspec jobs to catch style and logic issues on every PR.

children.title: Docker for Ruby apps
children.description: Multi-stage builds with ruby:slim images produce lean production containers — use BUNDLE_DEPLOYMENT=true to install only production gems in the final image.

php.title: PHP Syntax and Basics
php.description: Set up a local PHP environment, then learn the core language: variables and scope, PHP's type system and type juggling, strings, match expressions, arrays, and functions with named arguments, closures, and arrow functions. Turn on strict_types early so the engine catches type mistakes for you.
topics: Local setup with Docker or Herd
php.challenge: Build a CLI script with declare(strict_types=1) that reads student names and scores from an array, uses array_map/array_filter and a match expression to assign letter grades, and prints a formatted report. Run it inside the official php Docker image or Herd.

children.title: Local setup with Docker or Herd
children.description: You need a PHP binary and ideally a web server before writing any code. The official php Docker image gives you a pinned, reproducible version per project; Laravel Herd is a one-click native setup on macOS and Windows. Avoid old all-in-one bundles like XAMPP, which lag behind on PHP versions.

children.title: Variables, scope, and constants
children.description: PHP variables start with $ and are function-scoped: a function cannot see outer variables unless they are passed in or captured. Constants (const or define) cannot be reassigned, which makes configuration values safer. Knowing these rules early avoids the classic 'undefined variable' surprises.

children.title: Types and type juggling
children.description: PHP converts types implicitly in comparisons and arithmetic, so '10' == '1e1' is true. Use === for comparisons and add declare(strict_types=1) with typed parameters so mismatches throw instead of silently converting. This is the single biggest habit that separates modern PHP from legacy code.

resources.label: PHP Manual — Type declarations and strict typing

children.title: Strings and output
children.description: Single-quoted strings are literal, double-quoted and heredoc strings interpolate variables. echo and printf send output straight into the HTTP response, and the str_* and mb_* functions cover searching, slicing and multibyte text. Use mb_ functions whenever user text may contain non-ASCII characters.

children.title: Conditionals and match
children.description: if/elseif/else handles general branching. match (PHP 8.0) is an expression that compares strictly, returns a value, and throws if no arm matches, so it replaces most switch statements without the fall-through bugs.

children.title: Arrays
children.description: PHP's array is one ordered hash map that serves as list, dictionary, stack and queue. Learn array_map, array_filter, array_reduce, destructuring with [ ] and the spread operator, because they replace most hand-written loops in real code.

children.title: Functions: named args, defaults, variadics
children.description: Functions take typed parameters with defaults, variadic ...$args, and (since PHP 8.0) named arguments so calls like str_pad(string: $s, length: 10) read clearly and can skip optional parameters. Always declare parameter and return types.

children.title: Closures and arrow functions
children.description: Anonymous functions capture outer variables explicitly with use; arrow functions fn() => capture them automatically by value and are ideal for short callbacks to array_map or usort. First-class callable syntax strlen(...) turns any function into a Closure.

php.title: Forms, Superglobals, and HTTP
php.description: Learn how PHP sees an HTTP request through superglobals, how to validate input and escape output, and how sessions, cookies, file uploads, headers and redirects work. These are the building blocks every PHP framework wraps.
topics: include vs require and output escaping
php.challenge: Build a contact form with a profile-picture upload: validate every field with filter_var, re-render errors with escaped values, store the upload outside the web root with a random name, regenerate the session id on login, and use Post/Redirect/Get after a successful submit.

children.title: Superglobals and the request
children.description: PHP exposes the request through superglobals: $_GET for query strings, $_POST for form bodies, $_SERVER for method, headers and paths, $_FILES for uploads. They are always available in every scope, which is convenient but makes code hard to test, so frameworks wrap them in request objects.

children.title: Validating and sanitizing input
children.description: Treat every request value as untrusted and as a string. Validate type and range with filter_var (FILTER_VALIDATE_INT, FILTER_VALIDATE_EMAIL) and reject bad input instead of trying to clean it. Escaping belongs at output time, not input time.

children.title: Sessions and session fixation
children.description: session_start() gives each visitor a server-side store keyed by a cookie id. If you keep the same id across login, an attacker who planted that id owns the session, so call session_regenerate_id(true) whenever privileges change.

children.title: Cookies
children.description: setcookie() sends a Set-Cookie header, so it must run before any output. Use the options array to set HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite on every cookie; they block script access, plain-HTTP leaks and most cross-site sends.

children.title: File uploads
children.description: Uploaded files land in a temp directory and are described in $_FILES. Check the error code and size, detect the real type with finfo instead of trusting the client, generate your own file name, and move it with move_uploaded_file to a directory that the web server will not execute.

children.title: Headers and redirects
children.description: header() sets response headers and status codes and only works before output is sent. A redirect is header('Location: ...') plus exit. The Post/Redirect/Get pattern stops browsers from resubmitting a form on refresh.

children.title: include vs require
children.description: require stops the script with a fatal error if the file is missing; include only warns. The _once variants skip files already loaded. In modern code you use them mainly for templates and config, and let Composer's autoloader load classes.

children.title: Output escaping basics
children.description: Any user value echoed into HTML must go through htmlspecialchars($v, ENT_QUOTES) or the browser may run injected script. Escape for the context you print into: HTML, attribute, URL and JavaScript each need different encoding.

php.title: Object-Oriented PHP
php.description: Model code with classes: constructor promotion, inheritance and abstract classes, interfaces, traits, static members, final and magic methods. Organize classes with namespaces and autoloading, and use PHP 8.4 property hooks and asymmetric visibility instead of boilerplate getters and setters.

resources.label: PHP: The Right Way — Programming paradigms

php.challenge: Model a small library system: an interface for Borrowable items, an abstract Item base class, final Book and Dvd classes using constructor promotion, a trait for timestamps, and a property hook that validates an ISBN. Put everything in namespaces loaded by an autoloader.

children.title: Classes and constructor promotion
children.description: A class bundles typed properties with the methods that use them. Constructor promotion (PHP 8.0) declares and assigns properties straight from constructor parameters, removing most of the boilerplate that made older PHP classes long.

children.title: Inheritance and abstract classes
children.description: extends lets a class reuse and override a parent's behaviour; abstract classes define a partial implementation that cannot be instantiated. Keep hierarchies shallow and prefer composition, because deep inheritance makes changes ripple unpredictably.

children.title: Interfaces
children.description: An interface is a contract: a list of public methods a class promises to implement. Type-hinting against interfaces instead of concrete classes lets you swap implementations, which is how frameworks and test doubles work.

children.title: Traits
children.description: Traits copy methods and properties into a class, giving PHP horizontal reuse without multiple inheritance. They are handy for small cross-cutting helpers, but heavy trait use hides where behaviour comes from, so use them sparingly.

children.title: Static members and final
children.description: Static properties and methods belong to the class, not an instance; they suit factories and pure helpers but act like global state if overused. final stops a class or method from being extended or overridden, and is a good default for classes not designed for inheritance.

children.title: Magic methods
children.description: Methods like __construct, __toString, __get, __call and __invoke let PHP call into your class at special moments. They power ORMs and proxies, but magic property access hides typos from static analysis, so reach for them only when needed.

children.title: Namespaces and autoloading
children.description: Namespaces stop class-name collisions between your code and libraries. spl_autoload_register loads a class file the first time the class is used, and in practice Composer's PSR-4 autoloader does this for you based on namespace and folder.

children.title: Property hooks and asymmetric visibility (8.4)
children.description: PHP 8.4 lets a property define get and set hooks, so validation and computed values live on the property instead of in separate getter and setter methods. Asymmetric visibility (public private(set)) makes a property readable everywhere but writable only inside the class.

php.title: Composer and Dependency Management
php.description: Use Composer to install packages, lock exact versions, write version constraints, and autoload your own code with PSR-4. Learn Composer scripts, how to pick packages on Packagist, and how to optimize the autoloader and audit dependencies for production.
topics: Packagist, composer audit, and optimized autoloading
php.challenge: Turn your php-3 library system into a Composer project: PSR-4 autoload under src/, require a logging package with a caret constraint, add composer scripts for lint and test, commit composer.lock, and run composer audit plus an optimized install.

children.title: Composer basics
children.description: Composer is PHP's dependency manager: composer require adds a package, composer install reproduces the locked set, and vendor/autoload.php loads everything. It replaced copying libraries by hand and is assumed by every modern PHP project.

children.title: composer.json
children.description: composer.json declares your package name, PHP version, dependencies, dev dependencies, autoload rules and scripts. It is the source of truth for what your project needs, so keep it tidy and review changes to it like code.

children.title: composer.lock and reproducible installs
children.description: composer.lock records the exact version of every package that was resolved. Commit it for applications so every machine and deploy installs identical code; composer update is the only command that should change it.

children.title: Version constraints
children.description: Constraints like ^2.3 (any 2.x from 2.3) and ~2.3 tell Composer which updates are safe, relying on semantic versioning. Caret is the usual default because it accepts fixes and features but blocks breaking major versions.

children.title: PSR-4 autoloading
children.description: PSR-4 maps a namespace prefix to a directory, so App\Models\User lives in src/Models/User.php. Declare it once in composer.json and Composer loads every class on demand, with no require statements.

children.title: Optimized autoloader
children.description: In production, composer install --no-dev --optimize-autoloader builds a class map so PHP skips filesystem lookups. The authoritative class map goes further and never touches the disk for unknown classes.

children.title: Composer scripts
children.description: The scripts section names project commands such as composer test or composer lint and can hook into install and update events. It gives every contributor and CI the same entry points without a separate task runner.

children.title: Packagist and choosing packages
children.description: Packagist is the default package registry. Judge a package by maintenance activity, downloads, supported PHP versions and open security advisories, and run composer audit to check your lock file against known vulnerabilities.

php.title: Databases and PDO
php.description: Talk to SQL databases through PDO: connect with a DSN, turn on exception error mode, use prepared statements with bound parameters, pick the right fetch mode, wrap multi-step writes in transactions, and hide SQL behind a repository class.
php.challenge: Build a BookRepository on PDO for MySQL or SQLite with find, search, save and delete. Use only prepared statements, ERRMODE_EXCEPTION, FETCH_CLASS into a Book object, and a transaction that moves a book between two shelves atomically.

children.title: Connecting with PDO
children.description: PDO is one API for MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite and more; you pick the driver through the DSN string. Set charset=utf8mb4 for MySQL in the DSN, and create one connection per request instead of reconnecting in every function.

resources.label: PHP Manual — Connections and connection management

children.title: PDO error mode
children.description: Set PDO::ATTR_ERRMODE to PDO::ERRMODE_EXCEPTION so failed queries throw PDOException instead of returning false that nobody checks. It is the default since PHP 8.0, but setting it explicitly documents the intent.

resources.label: PHP Manual — Errors and error handling

children.title: Prepared statements
children.description: A prepared statement sends the SQL and the values separately, so user input can never change the query's structure. This is the fix for SQL injection; never build SQL by concatenating request values.

children.title: Named and positional parameters
children.description: Placeholders can be positional (?) or named (:email); named ones read better in long queries. Pass values to execute(), or use bindValue with a PDO::PARAM_* type when the type matters, such as LIMIT values.

children.title: Fetch modes
children.description: Fetch modes decide the shape of each row: FETCH_ASSOC for arrays, FETCH_COLUMN for a single list, FETCH_KEY_PAIR for id-to-name maps. Set a default with PDO::ATTR_DEFAULT_FETCH_MODE so you are not repeating it on every call.

children.title: Hydrating objects with FETCH_CLASS
children.description: FETCH_CLASS and fetchObject map columns straight onto a class's properties, giving you typed objects instead of loose arrays. This is the small-scale version of what ORMs like Eloquent and Doctrine do.

children.title: Transactions
children.description: beginTransaction, commit and rollBack group several writes so they all succeed or none do. Wrap them in try/catch and roll back on any exception, otherwise a half-finished transfer can leave your data inconsistent.

children.title: Repository class
children.description: A repository puts all SQL for one entity behind methods like find and save, and takes PDO through its constructor. The rest of the app depends on the repository, not on SQL, which keeps queries in one place and makes testing easier.

php.title: PSR Standards and Clean Architecture
php.description: Follow the PHP-FIG standards that let code and libraries fit together: PER Coding Style enforced by PHP CS Fixer, PSR-3 logging with Monolog, PSR-7 and PSR-15 for HTTP, and a clear exception and error-handling strategy built on Throwable.
topics: PSR-7 HTTP messages and PSR-15 middleware

resources.label: PHP: The Right Way — Errors and Exceptions

php.challenge: Add PHP CS Fixer with the @PER-CS ruleset to your Composer project, install Monolog behind a PSR-3 LoggerInterface, register global error and exception handlers that log with context and return a clean 500 page, and define domain exception classes for not-found and validation errors.

children.title: PER Coding Style
children.description: PER Coding Style is PHP-FIG's living style guide and replaces PSR-12, which stopped at PHP 7.3 syntax. It covers newer features like enums, attributes and match, so it is the standard to follow today.

children.title: PHP CS Fixer
children.description: PHP CS Fixer rewrites files to match a ruleset such as @PER-CS instead of only reporting problems. Run it in a pre-commit hook and in CI so style never comes up in code review.

children.title: PSR-7 HTTP messages
children.description: PSR-7 defines immutable request and response interfaces, so a library can work with any framework's HTTP objects. Every with* method returns a new object, which avoids hidden shared state.

children.title: PSR-15 middleware
children.description: PSR-15 standardizes handlers and middleware that take a PSR-7 request and return a response. Authentication, CORS and logging become small reusable layers that wrap your application.

children.title: Exceptions and Throwable
children.description: Since PHP 7, both Exception and engine Error implement Throwable. Throw specific exception classes for domain failures, catch them where you can actually recover, and let everything else reach a top-level handler.

children.title: Error levels and handlers
children.description: Warnings, notices and deprecations are separate from exceptions and are controlled by error_reporting. Use set_error_handler to convert them into ErrorException and set_exception_handler as the last line of defense, and never show raw errors in production.

children.title: PSR-3 logger interface
children.description: PSR-3 defines LoggerInterface with levels from debug to emergency and a context array for structured data. Depend on the interface, not a concrete logger, so you can swap implementations or use a null logger in tests.

children.title: Monolog in practice
children.description: Monolog is the PSR-3 logger used by Laravel and Symfony. Handlers decide where logs go (files, stderr, external services), formatters decide shape such as JSON, and processors add request ids or user ids to every entry.

php.title: Testing PHP Applications
php.description: Test PHP code with PHPUnit and Pest, isolate dependencies with test doubles, cover many cases with data providers, and catch bugs before running anything with PHPStan. Measure coverage and run it all in CI on every push.
php.challenge: Write a PHPUnit or Pest suite for your BookRepository and a service that uses it: data providers for validation rules, a mock repository for the service tests, PHPStan at level 6 or higher with no errors, and a GitHub Actions workflow that runs tests with coverage on two PHP versions.

children.title: Writing tests with PHPUnit
children.description: PHPUnit is the standard PHP test framework: test classes extend TestCase and use assertions like assertSame. Prefer assertSame over assertEquals because it compares strictly, matching the === habit from day one.

children.title: Data providers
children.description: A data provider feeds many input and expected-output rows into one test method. It keeps edge cases visible in a table instead of copy-pasted tests, and each row is reported separately when it fails.

children.title: Test doubles
children.description: Stubs return canned values; mocks also verify that certain calls happened. Use them for slow or external dependencies such as HTTP clients or mailers, and depend on interfaces so doubles are easy to create.

children.title: Pest
children.description: Pest is a test framework built on PHPUnit with a function-based syntax (it(), expect()) that reads closer to plain English. It is the default in new Laravel projects, while PHPUnit classes remain common elsewhere; both run the same way.

children.title: PHPStan
children.description: PHPStan reads your code without running it and finds type errors, undefined methods and impossible conditions. In a dynamically typed language it catches a large class of bugs that tests would only hit by luck.

children.title: Rule levels and baselines
children.description: PHPStan levels go from 0 (basic checks) to max (strict). On an existing codebase, generate a baseline to record current errors, then raise the level and only fail on new problems.

children.title: Code coverage
children.description: Coverage shows which lines your tests execute and needs a driver: PCOV is fast and coverage-only, Xdebug also debugs. Use coverage to find untested branches, not as a number to chase.

children.title: Running tests in CI
children.description: Run tests, PHPStan and the style check on every push. shivammathur/setup-php installs any PHP version and extension in GitHub Actions, so a matrix can test several PHP versions at once.

php.title: Modern PHP 8.x Features
php.description: Use the features that define modern PHP: union, intersection and DNF types, enums, readonly properties and classes, attributes, and fibers. Then catch up on PHP 8.4 (property hooks, new array functions, lazy objects) and the PHP 8.5 pipe operator.
php.challenge: Refactor your library project to modern PHP: replace status strings with a backed enum, make value objects readonly, add a custom attribute that marks routes and read it with reflection, and rewrite a data-processing chain with the pipe operator if you are on PHP 8.5.

children.title: Union and intersection types
children.description: Union types (int|string) accept any of several types; intersection types (Countable&Iterator) require all of them. Together they replace most docblock-only type hints with checks the engine enforces.

children.title: DNF, never, and mixed
children.description: PHP 8.2 allows DNF types like (A&B)|null. never marks functions that always throw or exit, and mixed explicitly accepts anything. Using them precisely gives PHPStan and readers exact information.

children.title: Enums
children.description: Enums (PHP 8.1) define a closed set of values; backed enums map each case to a string or int for storage. They replace class constants and magic strings, and match on an enum lets static analysis check you handled every case.

children.title: Readonly properties and classes
children.description: A readonly property can be set once, inside the class, and never changed. readonly classes (8.2) make every property readonly, which is the simplest way to build immutable value objects and DTOs.

children.title: Attributes
children.description: Attributes (#[Route('/books')]) attach structured metadata to classes, methods and properties, read through reflection. Frameworks use them for routing, validation and ORM mapping instead of parsing docblock annotations.

children.title: Fibers
children.description: Fibers (8.1) let code pause and resume without callbacks, the low-level primitive behind async libraries like ReactPHP and Amp. You rarely use them directly, but they explain how non-blocking PHP works.

children.title: What's new in PHP 8.4
children.description: PHP 8.4 added property hooks, asymmetric visibility, array_find and array_any, new without parentheses, and lazy objects. Reading each release page is the fastest way to keep your PHP current.

children.title: The pipe operator (8.5)
children.description: PHP 8.5's |> passes the value on its left into the callable on its right, so nested calls like trim(strtolower($s)) read left to right. It pairs naturally with first-class callables such as strtolower(...).

php.title: Security and Performance
php.description: Defend against the attacks that hit PHP apps most: XSS, SQL injection and CSRF. Store passwords with password_hash and generate secrets with random_bytes. Then make code fast with OPcache and JIT, cache data with APCu, and find real bottlenecks with the Xdebug profiler.
php.challenge: Harden and speed up your app: escape every template value, add CSRF tokens to all forms, migrate stored passwords to password_hash(PASSWORD_DEFAULT) with password_needs_rehash on login, enable OPcache, cache an expensive query in APCu, and use an Xdebug profile to prove the speedup.

children.title: Preventing XSS with htmlspecialchars
children.description: Cross-site scripting happens when user text is printed as HTML and runs as script in another user's browser. Escape all output with htmlspecialchars($v, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8') or a template engine that auto-escapes, such as Twig or Blade.

children.title: Preventing SQL injection
children.description: SQL injection lets attackers read or change any data by smuggling SQL through input. Prepared statements fix values; for dynamic column or sort names, use a whitelist because placeholders cannot bind identifiers.

children.title: CSRF protection
children.description: Cross-site request forgery tricks a logged-in browser into submitting a form to your site. Store a random token in the session, include it in every form, and compare with hash_equals; SameSite cookies add a second layer.

children.title: Password hashing with password_hash
children.description: Use password_hash($pw, PASSWORD_DEFAULT) and password_verify; PASSWORD_DEFAULT picks the current recommended algorithm and may change over time. Call password_needs_rehash after login so old hashes upgrade automatically. Never use md5 or sha1 for passwords.

children.title: Secure randomness with random_bytes
children.description: Tokens, reset links and API keys must be unguessable, so generate them with random_bytes or random_int, which use the OS cryptographic generator. rand, mt_rand and uniqid are predictable and unsafe for secrets.

children.title: OPcache and JIT
children.description: OPcache keeps compiled bytecode in shared memory so PHP does not re-parse files on every request; it is the biggest free speedup and must be on in production. JIT compiles hot code to machine code and mainly helps CPU-heavy work, not typical database-bound web requests.

resources.label: PHP Manual — OPcache and JIT configuration

children.title: APCu user cache
children.description: APCu stores your own values in shared memory on one server, ideal for caching config or expensive lookups. It is not shared across servers, so use Redis or Memcached when you run more than one instance.

children.title: Profiling with Xdebug
children.description: The Xdebug profiler records how long every function call takes, and tools like KCachegrind or QCachegrind visualize the result. Profile before optimizing, because the slow part is usually a query or loop you did not suspect.

php.title: Production PHP - APIs, Queues, and Deployment
php.description: Ship PHP to production: build JSON APIs with consistent errors, run background jobs through queues and workers, keep config and secrets in the environment, and serve PHP with PHP-FPM behind Nginx or with FrankenPHP. Package it in Docker and deploy through CI.

resources.label: PHP: The Right Way — Servers and Deployment

php.challenge: Expose your library app as a JSON API with RFC 9457 error responses, move email notifications to a queue worker, load config from environment variables, package it in a multi-stage Docker image (PHP-FPM + Nginx or FrankenPHP), and deploy it from a CI pipeline that runs tests first.

children.title: JSON in PHP
children.description: json_encode and json_decode convert between PHP values and JSON. Always pass JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR so malformed data throws instead of returning null silently, and set the Content-Type: application/json header on responses.

children.title: Designing a JSON API
children.description: A good API uses resource-based URLs, correct HTTP methods and status codes, and one consistent error format. RFC 9457 Problem Details is the standard error shape, so clients can handle failures without guessing.

resources.label: RFC 9457 — Problem Details for HTTP APIs

children.title: Queues and workers
children.description: Slow work like emails, image processing and webhooks should not block the HTTP response. Push a job onto a queue (Redis, a database, RabbitMQ) and process it with a long-running worker kept alive by a process supervisor.

children.title: Configuration and secrets
children.description: Keep config that changes between environments, especially secrets, in environment variables, not in code. A .env file loaded by phpdotenv is fine locally; in production, use the platform's secret store and never commit .env.

children.title: PHP-FPM and Nginx
children.description: The classic production setup: Nginx serves static files and forwards .php requests over FastCGI to a pool of PHP-FPM workers. Tune pm.max_children to your memory so the server does not swap under load.

children.title: FrankenPHP
children.description: FrankenPHP is a modern app server built on Caddy with automatic HTTPS and HTTP/3. Its worker mode boots your app once and keeps it in memory between requests, which is much faster but means you must avoid leaking state across requests.

children.title: Docker for PHP
children.description: Build from the official php image, install extensions with docker-php-ext-install, and use a multi-stage build so Composer and dev tools stay out of the final image. Pin the PHP version so production matches CI.

children.title: CI/CD pipelines
children.description: A pipeline runs style checks, PHPStan and tests on every push, builds the image, and deploys only when everything passes. Run composer install --no-dev --optimize-autoloader in the build, and run migrations as a separate, explicit step.

c.title: C Syntax and Compilation
c.description: Learn C syntax, integer types, operators, and the compilation pipeline from source to executable. Understand implicit conversions and operator precedence, and compile your first programs with GCC or Clang using modern flags: -std=c23, warnings on, and sanitizers enabled.
topics: Integer types, sizeof, and implicit conversions
Control flow: if, for, while, switch
Standard I/O with printf and scanf
c.challenge: Write a C program that reads integers from stdin, computes min, max, and average, then prints a formatted summary. Compile it with -std=c23 -Wall -Wextra -fsanitize=address,undefined and fix every warning.

children.title: Preprocessor, compiler, assembler, linker
children.description: C source goes through four stages: the preprocessor expands macros and #includes, the compiler produces assembly, the assembler produces object files, and the linker combines them into an executable.

children.title: Translation units and linkage
children.description: Each .c file is a separate translation unit compiled independently — external linkage (default for functions/globals) makes symbols visible across units; static restricts them to the current file.

children.title: Integer types, sizeof, and implicit conversions
children.description: int, long, and char have minimum sizes, not fixed ones, so sizeof tells you what you actually get on a platform. When types mix in an expression, C silently promotes and converts them, and comparing a signed value with an unsigned one is a classic source of bugs.

children.title: Bitwise operators and precedence
children.description: &, |, ^, ~, << and >> work on individual bits and are how C code handles flags, masks, and hardware registers. Their precedence is lower than you expect (x & 1 == 0 parses as x & (1 == 0)), so add parentheses whenever you mix them with comparisons.

children.title: GCC and Clang flags
children.description: A good default is -std=c23 -Wall -Wextra -g, plus -fsanitize=address,undefined while developing so memory errors and undefined behavior crash loudly instead of corrupting data. Add -Werror in CI and -O2 for release builds.

children.title: Make basics
children.description: A minimal Makefile with CC, CFLAGS, and a rule for each .o file handles most C project builds — make tracks dependencies and only recompiles changed files.

children.title: VS Code with clangd
children.description: clangd provides C-aware autocomplete, diagnostics, and go-to-definition — it reads compile_commands.json (generated by CMake or bear) for accurate project-wide analysis.

children.title: Compiler Explorer for C
children.description: godbolt.org shows the assembly output of any C snippet across GCC, Clang, and MSVC at different optimization levels — essential for understanding what your code compiles to.

c.title: Pointers and Memory Model
c.description: Understand the C memory model, pointer arithmetic, and the relationship between arrays and pointers. Write functions that operate on data via pointers.
c.challenge: Extend your statistics program to process data through pointer-based functions, passing arrays by pointer and returning results via output parameters.

children.title: Stack, heap, BSS, and data segments
children.description: C programs have four memory regions: stack (local variables, LIFO), heap (dynamic allocation), data segment (initialized globals), and BSS (zero-initialized globals) — knowing which region holds what prevents common bugs.

children.title: Pointer size and representation
children.description: A pointer holds a memory address — its size is 4 bytes on 32-bit systems, 8 bytes on 64-bit. Pointer arithmetic increments by sizeof(pointed-to type), not by 1 byte.

children.title: Dereferencing NULL and dangling pointers
children.description: Accessing memory through a NULL or freed pointer is undefined behavior — the program may crash, silently corrupt data, or behave differently under optimization.

children.title: Buffer overflows
children.description: Writing past the end of a stack or heap buffer overwrites adjacent memory — source of security vulnerabilities (stack smashing, heap corruption) and the #1 C bug class.

resources.label: Smashing the Stack for Fun and Profit

children.title: Valgrind for memory errors
children.description: valgrind --leak-check=full detects heap leaks, use-after-free, and invalid reads/writes at runtime — run it on every C program that does dynamic memory allocation.

children.title: AddressSanitizer (ASan)
children.description: Compile with -fsanitize=address to catch buffer overflows, use-after-free, and stack corruption at runtime with minimal overhead — faster feedback than Valgrind.

children.title: Pointer to pointer
children.description: char **argv is a pointer to a pointer — used for arrays of strings, output parameters, and linked data structures where you need to modify a pointer itself.

children.title: Function pointers
children.description: void (*callback)(int) declares a pointer to a function taking int — used for callbacks, dispatch tables, and implementing polymorphism in C without a class system.

c.title: Strings and Standard Library
c.description: Work with C strings as char arrays and use the standard library for string manipulation, memory allocation, and sorting. Understand null-termination and buffer safety.

resources.label: C Programming: A Modern Approach (K. N. King)
GNU C Library — String and Array Utilities

c.challenge: Add string-based input to your project: read a CSV of names and scores, parse numbers with strtol, dynamically allocate storage, build output with snprintf, and sort entries by score using qsort.

children.title: Null-terminated strings
children.description: C strings are arrays of char terminated by '\0' — no length field is stored, so every string operation (strlen, strcpy) must scan for the null terminator, making O(n) a hidden cost.

children.title: String literals and const char*
children.description: String literals live in read-only memory — char *s = "hello"; should be const char *s. Modifying a string literal is undefined behavior; modifying a char array copy is fine.

children.title: errno for error signaling
children.description: Standard library functions signal errors via errno (a thread-local global) and return -1 or NULL — always check the return value and errno immediately after a failing call.

children.title: Header-only declarations
children.description: C standard library headers declare functions but don't define them — the definitions live in libc, linked automatically. Understanding this explains why you include <string.h> but link nothing explicitly.

children.title: Safe string functions
children.description: strncpy is not a safe strcpy: if the source is too long it leaves the buffer without a '\0'. Prefer snprintf, which always terminates and reports the length it needed, or strlcpy where available (BSD, macOS, glibc 2.38+). The C11 Annex K _s functions are optional and unsupported by glibc, so don't rely on them.

children.title: strtol and strtod for parsing
children.description: strtol converts strings to integers with error detection via endptr and errno — safer than atoi which silently returns 0 on failure.

children.title: qsort and bsearch
children.description: qsort sorts any array with a custom comparator function pointer; bsearch performs binary search — both work on any data type through void* and size parameters.

children.title: malloc, calloc, realloc, free
children.description: malloc allocates uninitialized memory; calloc zero-initializes; realloc resizes — always check for NULL return and always free every allocated block exactly once.

c.title: Structs, Unions, and Enums
c.description: Group related data using structs, model variant types with unions, and improve readability with enums and typedef. Build linked data structures.
c.challenge: Refactor your data model into structs representing students and score records, link them in a singly-linked list, and implement insert and search operations.

children.title: Struct padding and alignment
children.description: The compiler inserts padding between struct members to satisfy alignment requirements — a struct with char, int can be 8 bytes, not 5. Use offsetof() to measure layout.

children.title: Flexible array members
children.description: struct { int len; char data[]; } uses a flexible array member — the array has no size in the struct definition, and malloc(sizeof(struct) + n) allocates n extra bytes for it.

children.title: Union memory layout
children.description: All union members share the same memory — a union is as large as its largest member. Used for type-punning, variant types, and memory-efficient data representation.

children.title: Tagged unions for sum types
children.description: Combining a union with an enum tag creates a discriminated union (variant type) — the standard C pattern for representing values that can be one of several types.

children.title: Opaque pointers for encapsulation
children.description: Exposing only typedef struct MyType* MyType in a header (with implementation in the .c file) hides the struct layout — callers can't access fields directly, enforcing encapsulation.

children.title: Designated initializers
children.description: struct Point p = { .x = 1.0, .y = 2.0 } initializes by field name — safer than positional initialization, immune to reordering bugs, and self-documenting.

children.title: Bit field structs
children.description: struct Flags { unsigned int ready: 1; unsigned int error: 1; } packs multiple flags into a single int — used in hardware registers, network protocol headers, and memory-constrained embedded systems.

children.title: __attribute__((packed))
children.description: GCC's packed attribute removes all struct padding — useful for serialization and hardware register mapping where layout must exactly match a specification.

c.title: File I/O and Error Handling
c.description: Read and write files using FILE streams and handle errors robustly using errno and return-code conventions. Implement resource cleanup on all exit paths.
topics: Cleanup with goto or nested ifs

resources.label: Beej's Guide to C — File I/O
C Programming: A Modern Approach (K. N. King)

c.challenge: Persist your linked list to a binary file, reload it on startup, and handle all fopen and fread errors with descriptive messages and clean exits.

children.title: FILE* and buffered I/O
children.description: FILE* is a buffered I/O stream — fread/fwrite transfer data through an internal buffer, batching syscalls for performance. fflush forces the buffer to the OS.

resources.label: Beej's Guide to C — File I/O

children.title: Binary vs text mode
children.description: Text mode translates line endings (\r\n on Windows); binary mode transfers bytes unchanged — always use binary mode for non-text data to prevent silent corruption.

children.title: Return value conventions
children.description: C functions signal errors through return values — 0 for success (or -1 for failure) for most functions, NULL for pointer-returning functions. Always check every return value.

children.title: setjmp/longjmp for non-local jumps
children.description: setjmp saves the current execution context and longjmp jumps back to it, which some C libraries use for error recovery, a bit like exceptions. It is dangerous because longjmp skips all cleanup in the frames it unwinds: nothing is freed, closed, or unlocked.

children.title: fseek, ftell, rewind
children.description: fseek positions the file cursor; ftell returns the current position; rewind resets to the beginning — used together for random access within files.

children.title: POSIX file descriptors vs FILE*
children.description: POSIX open/read/write/close operate on integer file descriptors (unbuffered); FILE* wraps them with buffering — use FILE* for most file operations, fd for sockets and low-level I/O.

children.title: perror and strerror
children.description: perror("context") prints the error message for the current errno to stderr; strerror(errno) returns it as a string — always use them to give context to error messages.

children.title: Cleanup on error with goto
children.description: The goto cleanup pattern — allocate resources, jump to a cleanup label on any error — is the idiomatic C way to ensure all resources are freed without deeply nested if checks.

c.title: Makefiles and Build Systems
c.description: Organize a multi-file C project with header files and a Makefile that supports incremental builds, compiler warnings, and release and debug targets.
topics: Header guards, macros, and conditional compilation
Makefile rules, variables, and phony targets
c.challenge: Split your project into modules (io, list, stats) each with its own .c and .h file, and write a Makefile with debug and release targets and automatic dependency tracking.

children.title: Rules, targets, and prerequisites
children.description: A Makefile rule has the form target: prerequisites; recipe — Make rebuilds a target only when a prerequisite is newer, tracking dependencies through file modification times.

children.title: Automatic variables
children.description: $@ is the target name, $< is the first prerequisite, $^ is all prerequisites — these variables make generic pattern rules reusable across all source files.

children.title: Optimization levels -O0 to -O3
children.description: -O0 no optimization (debug); -O1 basic optimizations; -O2 standard production; -O3 aggressive (may increase size). -Os optimizes for size, -Og for debug-friendly optimization.

children.title: Link-time optimization (LTO)
children.description: -flto enables link-time optimization — the linker can inline and optimize across translation unit boundaries, catching dead code that intra-file analysis misses.

children.title: Dependency generation with -MMD
children.description: gcc -MMD -MP generates .d files containing header dependencies — include them in the Makefile so changing a header triggers recompilation of all dependent .c files.

children.title: CMake for cross-platform builds
children.description: CMake generates native build files (Makefile, Ninja, Visual Studio) from a platform-independent CMakeLists.txt — the standard for C projects that need to build on multiple platforms.

children.title: Include guards and #pragma once
children.description: #ifndef MY_HEADER_H / #define MY_HEADER_H / #endif prevents double-inclusion of headers — #pragma once is simpler and supported by all major compilers.

children.title: Macros and conditional compilation
children.description: #define creates object-like constants and function-like macros that are pasted in as text before compilation, so always wrap macro arguments and bodies in parentheses. #if, #ifdef and #elif switch code on or off per platform or build type, for example debug logging only when DEBUG is defined.

c.title: Debugging with gdb and Valgrind
c.description: Debug C programs using gdb for step-through inspection and Valgrind for memory error detection. Eliminate leaks, use-after-free, and buffer overruns.
c.challenge: Intentionally introduce a memory bug into your project, then use Valgrind and gdb to locate and fix it, documenting each step.

children.title: How gdb works
children.description: gdb attaches to a process via ptrace, sets breakpoints by replacing instructions with INT3 (trap), and reads program state through /proc — understanding this helps you use gdb effectively.

children.title: Debug information and DWARF
children.description: The -g flag embeds DWARF debug info in the binary — source line numbers, variable names, and type information that gdb uses to map machine instructions back to C source.

children.title: Valgrind internals
children.description: Valgrind runs your program on a synthetic CPU that shadows every memory operation — it tracks which bytes are initialized and allocated, catching errors that ASan might miss.

children.title: Core dumps for post-mortem debugging
children.description: A core dump captures the full process state at crash time — gdb program core loads it for post-mortem analysis, examining the stack trace and variable values at the moment of failure.

children.title: Essential gdb commands
children.description: break, run, next, step, continue, print, backtrace, watch — these ten commands cover 95% of interactive debugging sessions in C.

children.title: TUI mode and gdb dashboard
children.description: gdb -tui shows source alongside commands; gdb-dashboard is a Python extension that adds a rich terminal UI with registers, memory, and variables — both dramatically improve debugging speed.

children.title: UBSan for undefined behavior
children.description: -fsanitize=undefined catches integer overflow, null dereference, misaligned access, and dozens of other UB cases at runtime — run alongside ASan for comprehensive coverage.

children.title: ThreadSanitizer for data races
children.description: -fsanitize=thread detects data races in multithreaded C programs — instruments all memory accesses and reports races with the thread IDs and stack traces involved.

c.title: Dynamic Data Structures and Algorithms
c.description: Implement common data structures from scratch in C: dynamic arrays, hash tables, and binary trees. Analyze time and space complexity of each.
c.challenge: Replace the linked list in your project with a hash table keyed by student ID, and add a binary search tree for sorted traversal by score.

children.title: Intrusive linked lists
children.description: Embedding a struct node { struct node *next; } directly in data structs (instead of a node wrapping a void*) avoids double allocation — used in the Linux kernel and many embedded systems.

children.title: Hash table design
children.description: A simple open-addressing hash table needs a hash function, a probe sequence for collisions, and a load factor limit for rehashing — understanding these choices explains STL and Redis internals.

children.title: void* for type-erased generics
children.description: C achieves generics with void* — qsort and bsearch use void* with a size parameter and function pointer comparator. The caller casts to the correct type, accepting the loss of type safety.

children.title: _Generic for type-safe dispatch
children.description: C11's _Generic macro dispatches to different expressions based on type at compile time — enables type-safe generic APIs without void* casts.

children.title: Sorting algorithms in C
children.description: Implementing quicksort with a median-of-three pivot and insertion sort fallback for small arrays matches the quality of most standard library implementations — a practical study in C optimization.

children.title: Memory pools for allocation
children.description: Allocating a large block upfront and carving it into fixed-size chunks (a memory pool) avoids malloc overhead and fragmentation — essential for embedded systems and high-performance servers.

children.title: Binary search tree in C
children.description: struct Node { int val; struct Node *left, *right; } is the recursive BST definition — implementing insert, search, and delete in C teaches pointer manipulation and recursive thinking.

children.title: Graph adjacency list
children.description: Representing a graph as an array of linked lists (adjacency list) is memory-efficient for sparse graphs — the standard C representation for BFS, DFS, and shortest path algorithms.

c.title: Systems Programming - Processes, Sockets, and Threads
c.description: Use POSIX APIs to spawn processes, handle signals, communicate over TCP sockets, and run work on threads. Understand file descriptors, the Unix process model, and how to protect shared data with mutexes and C11 atomics.
topics: TCP sockets: bind, listen, accept, connect
c.challenge: Turn your stats project into a client-server app: a server that accepts TCP connections and handles each client on its own pthread, protecting the shared statistics with a mutex, and a client that sends queries.

children.title: fork and exec
children.description: fork creates a copy of the current process; exec replaces the current process image with a new program — together they implement shell pipelines and process spawning in Unix.

children.title: Signals and signal handlers
children.description: Signals (SIGINT, SIGTERM, SIGSEGV) are asynchronous notifications — signal handlers must be async-signal-safe (no malloc, printf, or locks) as they can interrupt any point in the program.

children.title: TCP socket lifecycle
children.description: socket → bind → listen → accept (server) / socket → connect (client) → send/recv → close — each step has specific error conditions and blocking behavior to understand.

children.title: select and poll for I/O multiplexing
children.description: select/poll monitor multiple file descriptors for readiness — enabling a single-threaded server to handle many connections without blocking on any one of them.

children.title: Pipes and FIFOs
children.description: pipe(fds) creates a unidirectional byte stream between parent and child — the kernel buffers data between writes and reads, making pipes the simplest IPC mechanism.

children.title: Shared memory and semaphores
children.description: mmap with MAP_SHARED or POSIX shm_open shares memory between processes — combine with sem_wait/sem_post for synchronization to prevent races on shared data.

children.title: Beej's Guide to Network Programming
children.description: The definitive free resource for C socket programming — covers TCP/UDP, IPv4/IPv6, getaddrinfo, and non-blocking sockets with working C examples throughout.

children.title: epoll for high-performance servers
children.description: epoll (Linux) is O(1) for event notification across thousands of file descriptors — the foundation of nginx, Redis, and Node.js's event loops. kevent on BSD/macOS is equivalent.

children.title: POSIX threads: create and join
children.description: pthread_create starts a function on a new thread that shares the process's memory, and pthread_join waits for it to finish and collects its result. Every thread you create must be joined or detached, or its resources leak. Compile and link with -pthread.

children.title: Mutexes and C11 atomics
children.description: When two threads touch the same data and at least one writes, you have a data race, which is undefined behavior. Guard shared state with a pthread_mutex_t, or use C11 <stdatomic.h> types for simple counters and flags that need no lock. Run ThreadSanitizer to find the races you missed.

c.title: Production C - Modern C23, Testing, Profiling, and Embedding
c.description: Write portable, production-quality C targeting C23, with CMake builds, unit tests run by CTest, profiling tools, sanitizers, and static analysis. Learn the modern C23 features and how to ship C as a shared library that other languages call.
topics: CMake project structure and CTest unit tests
Calling C from Python via ctypes
c.challenge: Package your client-server project as a CMake build with -std=c23, add Unity unit tests run by CTest, profile it with perf to find bottlenecks, expose the stats engine as a shared library, and call it from a Python script via ctypes.

children.title: C standards: C89, C99, C11, C17, C23
children.description: C99 added // comments, stdint.h, and designated initializers; C11 added _Atomic, _Generic, and threads.h; C17 only fixed defects. C23 is the current standard and the default in GCC 15, so target -std=c23 for new code and fall back to -std=c17 when an older compiler or platform requires it.

children.title: Fixed-width integer types
children.description: stdint.h provides int8_t, int32_t, uint64_t etc. — use them instead of int or long when the exact size matters (network protocols, file formats, hardware registers).

children.title: gprof for function-level profiling
children.description: Compile with -pg and run the program — gprof generates a call graph and per-function timing. Less accurate than perf but requires no root access or kernel support.

children.title: perf for hardware counter profiling
children.description: perf stat counts CPU cycles, cache misses, and branch mispredictions — perf record + perf report generates flamegraphs. No recompilation needed; works on any binary.

children.title: nullptr, bool, and constexpr
children.description: C23 makes bool, true and false real keywords, adds nullptr as a typed null pointer constant that replaces the NULL macro, and adds constexpr for named compile-time constants that are safer than #define. Together they remove some of C's oldest macro workarounds.

children.title: #embed, typeof, and checked arithmetic
children.description: #embed pulls a binary file's bytes straight into an array at compile time, typeof is now standard for writing type-generic macros, and <stdckdint.h> gives ckd_add, ckd_sub and ckd_mul, which report integer overflow instead of triggering undefined behavior.

children.title: Static vs dynamic linking
children.description: Static linking (-static) copies libraries into the binary, so it runs anywhere with no runtime dependencies. Dynamic linking loads shared .so/.dll files at startup, giving smaller binaries and shared security updates at the cost of deployment complexity.

children.title: Embedding C in other languages
children.description: C is the universal FFI target — Python's ctypes, Lua's C API, Ruby's FFI, and Rust's FFI all call C functions. Designing a clean C API enables your library to be used from any language.

children.title: Unit tests with CTest and Unity
children.description: C has no built-in test runner, so a small framework like Unity gives you assertions and a test main. Register each test executable with add_test in CMake and ctest runs them all, which is also the one command your CI job calls, ideally once per sanitizer build.

children.title: cppcheck for static analysis
children.description: cppcheck finds memory leaks, null dereferences, and undefined behavior statically, without running the program. It complements runtime sanitizers and is cheap enough to run on every commit.

kotlin.title: Kotlin Syntax and Basics
kotlin.description: Learn Kotlin syntax, type inference, and basic constructs, including control flow as expressions, labeled returns, and exceptions. Understand how Kotlin differs from Java with its concise and expressive style, and know that current Kotlin (2.x) is built on the faster K2 compiler.
topics: Basic types, arrays, and type inference
Control flow: if, when, loops, and labels
Exceptions and try as an expression
Functions, default arguments, and null safety overview
kotlin.challenge: Write a Kotlin command-line app that reads a list of task strings, filters by a keyword, sorts alphabetically, and prints them with indices. Parse a priority number for each task using try as an expression so bad input falls back to a default instead of crashing.

children.title: 100% Java interoperability
children.description: Kotlin compiles to JVM bytecode and can call Java code directly — every Java library works in Kotlin without wrappers, and Kotlin can be adopted incrementally in existing Java projects.

children.title: Conciseness and safety
children.description: Kotlin eliminates boilerplate (no semicolons, type inference, data classes) while adding null safety and immutability — the same logic typically requires 40% fewer lines than Java.

children.title: Nullable and non-nullable types
children.description: String is non-null by default; String? is nullable — the type system enforces null safety at compile time, eliminating NullPointerExceptions structurally.

children.title: Type inference
children.description: Kotlin infers variable types from initializers — val name = "Alice" infers String. Function return types can also be inferred for single-expression functions.

children.title: Returns, breaks, and labels
children.description: In Kotlin, a bare return inside a lambda returns from the enclosing function, which surprises people coming from Java. Labels like return@forEach or break@outer let you say exactly which lambda or loop you are leaving.

children.title: Exceptions and try as an expression
children.description: Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so the compiler never forces you to catch anything. try, if, and when are expressions that return values, which lets you write val n = try { s.toInt() } catch (e: NumberFormatException) { 0 } instead of a mutable variable.

children.title: Arrays vs lists
children.description: Array is a fixed-size, mutable, JVM-array-backed type you mostly need for interop or primitive performance (IntArray). For everyday code, prefer List and MutableList, which have richer APIs and a read-only view by default.

children.title: IntelliJ IDEA and Kotlin plugin
children.description: IntelliJ IDEA has first-class Kotlin support built in — the same IDE that created Kotlin. The free Community edition is sufficient for Kotlin development outside Android.

children.title: Kotlin REPL and Scratch files
children.description: IntelliJ's Kotlin REPL and scratch files let you experiment with Kotlin expressions without creating a project — ideal for learning new APIs or testing snippets quickly.

children.title: The K2 compiler
children.description: Kotlin 2.0 shipped K2, a rewritten compiler frontend that compiles faster and makes smart casts work in more places. It is the default now, so new projects get it automatically; older projects may need small fixes when upgrading.

children.title: Gradle with Kotlin DSL
children.description: Kotlin DSL (build.gradle.kts) replaces Groovy for Gradle builds — statically typed, with autocomplete and refactoring support in the IDE.

children.title: Maven with Kotlin
children.description: kotlin-maven-plugin compiles Kotlin in Maven projects — useful for migrating existing Maven Java projects to Kotlin without switching build tools.

kotlin.title: Null Safety and Type System
kotlin.description: Master Kotlin null safety with nullable types, the Elvis operator, and safe calls. Understand smart casts and sealed classes for exhaustive type handling.
topics: Nullable types and safe call operator
Smart casts with is and as
kotlin.challenge: Add optional metadata to your task app using nullable types, handle missing fields with Elvis operators, and model task status as a sealed class.

children.title: Platform types from Java
children.description: Java types interoperating with Kotlin are 'platform types' (String!) — neither nullable nor non-null. Annotating Java with @Nullable/@NonNull makes the boundary type-safe.

children.title: Safe calls vs non-null assertion
children.description: ?. returns null if the receiver is null (safe); !! throws NPE if null (non-null assertion, should be rare) — prefer safe calls and let/also/run scope functions over !!.

children.title: Compiler-tracked type narrowing
children.description: After an is check, Kotlin automatically casts the variable to the checked type — no explicit cast needed, unlike Java's (Type) cast.

children.title: when expressions as smart cast triggers
children.description: when(x) { is String -> x.length } uses smart casting inside each branch — combined with sealed classes, when becomes exhaustive type dispatch.

children.title: Elvis operator ?:
children.description: val name = user?.name ?: "Guest" returns the right side if the left is null — the Kotlin equivalent of Java's Optional.orElse() without the wrapper type.

children.title: let, run, also, apply scope functions
children.description: ?.let { } executes a block only when non-null and receives the value as it — the idiomatic way to transform nullable values without null checks.

children.title: filterNotNull()
children.description: listOfNullables.filterNotNull() returns a List<T> from a List<T?> — type-safe filtering that removes nulls and narrows the element type at compile time.

children.title: requireNotNull and checkNotNull
children.description: requireNotNull(value) { "message" } throws IllegalArgumentException on null; checkNotNull throws IllegalStateException — use them to assert preconditions clearly.

kotlin.title: OOP - Classes, Data Classes, and Objects
kotlin.description: Use Kotlin classes, data classes, object declarations, and delegation to build concise and idiomatic OOP code. Learn why classes are final by default, how visibility works, when to pick an enum over a sealed class, and how generics with in/out variance keep APIs type-safe.
kotlin.challenge: Model your task app entities as data classes, use a companion object for factory methods, and implement interface delegation for pluggable storage backends. Make the storage interface generic (Repository<T>) and use an enum for priority and a sealed class for task status.

children.title: Generated methods
children.description: data class generates equals(), hashCode(), toString(), copy(), and componentN() functions based on constructor properties — replacing hundreds of lines of boilerplate Java.

children.title: copy() for immutable updates
children.description: val updated = user.copy(name = "Bob") creates a new instance with one field changed — the idiomatic Kotlin way to work with immutable data without mutation.

children.title: object for singletons
children.description: object declarations create thread-safe singletons lazily — no getInstance() or double-checked locking needed, the compiler guarantees a single instance.

children.title: companion object vs static
children.description: companion object {} groups class-level functions and constants — accessed as Class.method(), they compile to Java static members for interoperability.

children.title: Primary and secondary constructors
children.description: Primary constructor params can be val/var to define properties directly — secondary constructors must delegate to the primary with this().

children.title: Sealed classes for ADTs
children.description: sealed class restricts subclasses to the same file — with when expressions, sealed classes enable exhaustive pattern matching over a fixed set of types.

children.title: Class delegation with by
children.description: class LoggingList<T>(inner: MutableList<T>) : MutableList<T> by inner automatically delegates all interface methods to inner — implementing the decorator pattern with zero boilerplate.

children.title: Property delegation with by lazy
children.description: val heavy by lazy { expensiveInit() } defers initialization until first access and caches the result — thread-safe by default, with configurable synchronization modes.

children.title: open, abstract, and interfaces
children.description: Kotlin classes and members are final unless marked open, which pushes you toward composition and avoids fragile base classes. Use an abstract class when subclasses share state, and an interface (which can have default methods but no state) for a capability many types implement.

children.title: Visibility modifiers
children.description: Kotlin has public (the default), private, protected, and internal. internal means visible inside the same module, which is how libraries hide implementation details without Java's package-private tricks.

children.title: Enum classes vs sealed classes
children.description: An enum is a fixed set of single instances, good for plain options like Priority.HIGH. A sealed class is a fixed set of subtypes that can each carry different data, good for states like Loading, Success(data), Error(message). Both make when exhaustive.

children.title: Generics and variance (in/out)
children.description: Generics let one class work with many types safely. out T means a type only produces T (like List<out T>), so a List<Cat> can be used as a List<Animal>; in T means it only consumes T. This declaration-site variance replaces most of Java's wildcard syntax.

kotlin.title: Functional Programming and Collections
kotlin.description: Apply functional programming with Kotlin lambdas, higher-order functions, and the collections API. Use sequences for lazy evaluation of large datasets.
topics: Scope functions: let, run, with, apply, also
kotlin.challenge: Rewrite all data manipulation in your task app using Kotlin collection operations - group tasks by category, compute stats, and chain operations with sequences.

children.title: Higher-order functions
children.description: Functions that accept or return functions are first-class in Kotlin — inline modifier eliminates the lambda object allocation overhead for performance-critical higher-order functions.

children.title: inline functions and reified types
children.description: inline copies the function body to the call site; reified T makes the generic type available at runtime — enabling typeOf<T>() and is T checks inside inline generics.

children.title: Sequence vs Collection operations
children.description: Collection operations are eager — each step creates an intermediate list. Sequence operations are lazy — they chain into a single pass, like Java Streams.

children.title: generateSequence for infinite sequences
children.description: generateSequence(0) { it + 1 } creates an infinite sequence — take(n) or takeWhile limits consumption. Useful for pagination, fibonacci, or any recursive pattern.

children.title: map, filter, flatMap, groupBy
children.description: Kotlin's collection stdlib has 150+ extension functions — map transforms, filter selects, flatMap flattens, groupBy partitions into a Map<K, List<V>>.

children.title: associate, zip, and partition
children.description: associate transforms to a Map; zip pairs two lists element-wise; partition splits into a Pair<List, List> — three operations that replace common manual iteration patterns.

children.title: Trailing lambda syntax
children.description: When the last parameter is a function, the lambda can go outside the parentheses — list.filter { it > 0 } is cleaner than list.filter({ it > 0 }).

children.title: it and destructuring in lambdas
children.description: Single-parameter lambdas use it by default; multi-parameter lambdas can destructure: map.forEach { (k, v) -> } — both reduce verbosity for common patterns.

kotlin.title: Extension Functions and DSLs
kotlin.description: Extend existing classes without inheritance using extension functions and properties. Build internal DSLs with lambda receivers and infix functions.
kotlin.challenge: Create a task-builder DSL using lambda receivers so tasks can be constructed with a clean block syntax, and add extension functions on List<Task> for common queries.

children.title: Static dispatch at compile time
